## D-016 — The vendored `ziffle` is forked

Taken 2026-08-29. Closes `ZR-1`, which the verdict raised and explicitly declined
to decide, because it is a project-shape decision and not a cryptographic one.

### The decision

**Fork.** `vendor/ziffle/` is no longer the crates.io 0.1.0 tarball. The four
changes of condition C-12 are applied, each marked `FORK(x)` in the source and
each recorded in `vendor/ziffle/PROVENANCE.md`.

### Why now rather than later

Every item is a **wire-format** change, and the wire format is frozen by the
first proof that is persisted or exchanged. Before that, the change costs a
morning; after it, it costs a migration with two mutually unverifiable halves of
the network in the middle. There is no third moment at which this gets cheaper.

The two that force it:

* the transcript framed its lengths with `usize::to_be_bytes()`, eight bytes on
  x86-64 and four on wasm32, so two clients of different word widths derive
  different challenges from the same statement and neither can verify the
  other's proofs — a certain break the day anything runs in a browser;
* `RevealTokenProof` bound a card's first ciphertext coordinate and dropped the
  second, so a token issued for one card opened every card sharing that
  coordinate, and a malicious shuffler can arrange the collision. Demonstrated
  end to end at 52 cards.

Neither is a break of Bayer–Groth. Both are the library proving exactly what it
claims where the claim is not what a poker game needs.

### What it costs, stated plainly

* We are on a **private wire format** that no upstream fix will match. An
  upstream release is now a merge, not an upgrade.
* ziffle's own 16 unit tests and 15 doctests are no longer a check on the code we
  run without re-verification. They were re-run after the fork and pass; that has
  to happen after every future change, and `PROVENANCE.md` says so.
* Interoperability with the one other project using the crate is forfeited. It
  was never a goal, and this makes it a non-goal on the record.

### What did not change, deliberately

The verdict listed, as optional, deriving both sub-challenges from one joint
transcript state. **It is not done.** Two reviewers independently found the
existing fork to be the paper's own parallel composition and sound.
Restructuring something a review found sound is risk without benefit, and a
review is only worth having if its positive findings are respected as well as
its negative ones.

### What this does not decide

The verdict's §6 bar for **real money** is untouched and unmet: nobody proved
witness-extended emulation, and nobody re-derived the soundness bound at `m = 1`.
The fork makes the library fit for the play-money MVP under conditions C-1 to
C-15. It does not move the other bar an inch, and no amount of engineering time
buys items 1, 2, 3 and 6 of that list.

## D-017 — Surviving a disconnection mid-hand: **analysed, and withdrawn**

**Status: WITHDRAWN by the owner on 2026-08-29, the same day it was raised.
Nothing here is to be built.** What ships is the fallback that already exists:
heads-up needs no mechanism at all, and multi-way the hand aborts with `T46`
restoring every stack to its start-of-hand value.

The analysis is kept rather than deleted for two reasons. It records that
sharing **key** shares with outside nodes is unsafe, so nobody arrives at it
again by the obvious route; and it records the one correction that would make a
variant of it sound, so if the question returns the work does not start from
nothing.

Raised by the owner as two proposals. The first would have been adoptable with
one correction that is the whole of why it is safe; the second is declined
outright and would stay declined.

### What was already solved, and is worth stating first

**Heads-up, a rage quit needs no cryptography at all.** The absent seat auto
check/folds (D-006), `only_one_live` awards the pot, and — in that function's own
words — *the survivor wins every pot it is eligible for and never reveals a
card*. Nothing is decrypted because nothing has to be.

The gap is narrower than it first looks: **three or more seats, one gone, two
still in at showdown.** The board needs a reveal token from every key in the
aggregate, and one of them has left. That is where `n`-of-`n` bites, and it is the
only place it does.

### The correction: share tokens, not key shares

The proposal was to give outside nodes `t`-of-`n` shares of the **deck key**. That
does not work and `SPEC_CS.md` §35 already says so — *n-of-n stands; abort
neutrally*. The reason is worth writing down rather than citing:

**A share of the key is a share of the key.** Every card sits under one aggregate
key, so there is no construction that grants the ability to open index 12 and
withholds index 3. *"They only decrypt the board"* is a policy, and the nodes hold
what is needed to ignore it. Three colluding helpers read hole cards. And §18
places Sybil-without-identity outside the threat model, so an attacker may
simply **be** all five helpers.

**Sharing the five board reveal tokens instead inverts every one of those
properties:**

| | shares of the key | shares of the board tokens |
|---|---|---|
| three colluding helpers get | the key, hence hole cards | five values that open nothing alone |
| helpers plus one seated player | everything | still nothing — the other seat's token is missing |
| Sybil across all helpers | fatal | **harmless** |

The remaining players still gate each other: `n`-of-`n` among those **present**
holds unchanged. Even helpers who publish their shares at hand start achieve
nothing, because the board still cannot open before its street without the other
seat's token. And the departing player's own hole cards are untouched — the
helpers hold nothing about them, by construction rather than by promise.

### Why this and not simply "publish your tokens as you leave"

The simpler form — a client publishes its five board tokens as its last act —
handles a **graceful** exit and nothing else. A power cut, a crash or a killed
process publishes nothing, and those are exactly the cases the rule exists for.
Shares distributed at hand **start** survive all of them.

### The condition, which is the owner's, and it is load-bearing rather than tidy

**Only when helpers are reachable, and only helpers who are not seated in this
hand.** Both halves are the owner's and the second is the one that carries
weight, so it is worth being precise about why — the first reading of it was that
it is good hygiene, and it is not: without it the scheme is a break.

**Seated helpers collapse the gate.** Suppose seats `A`, `B` and `C`, and `C`
shares its board tokens with `A` and `B`. `A` and `B` between them now hold their
own tokens **and** `C`'s, which is every token the board needs. They can open the
flop, the turn and the river **before a single bet is made**, while `C` is still
sitting at the table playing. That is not a degradation of the property; it is
`SPEC_CS.md` §35's main invariant — *no participant may learn the future board* —
failing outright.

Two further reasons, either sufficient on its own:

* **A seated helper shares the failure domain.** The common cause of a
  disconnection is a router, an ISP or a Wi-Fi link, and the whole point of the
  helpers is to survive the event that removed the player. Helpers inside the
  same table are hit by the same table's trouble.
* **A seated helper has an interest in the outcome.** A player-helper can decline
  to reconstruct precisely when reconstructing would hand the pot to somebody
  else. A disinterested node has no reason to withhold, which is the only sense
  in which it is more trustworthy — and it is enough.

**With no eligible helpers, the fallback is the one already built:** the hand
aborts and `T46` restores every stack to its start-of-hand value, so no chip
crosses between seats and the tournament plays on. A mechanism that cannot be
attempted is not a mechanism that fails.

### What it still needs, and it is not optional

Verifiable secret sharing — Feldman or Pedersen over the same group — so that a
malicious departing player cannot distribute garbage and reach the same abort by
a longer route. That is an established, peer-reviewed construction and is
therefore admissible under §36; a hand-rolled sharing scheme here would not be.

### The second proposal is declined: time-lock puzzles

**The puzzle protects a *board* token, and sequential-squaring difficulty is
measured in the fastest available multiplier, not in the holder's.** An opponent
with better hardware opens the lock before that street arrives, and knowing the
river during flop betting is a total break of the game. The mechanism hands the
advantage to whoever has the faster processor, which is the opposite of its
purpose.

Two further reasons, either sufficient on its own:

* The modulus is generated by the party asserting the difficulty. A cheat picks
  one with a shortcut. Provable difficulty needs a VDF with a trusted setup or
  class groups, which is research-grade work.
* It is not needed for the case that motivated it. Heads-up is already solved by
  D-006, and multi-way is solved above without any new cryptographic assumption.

**No mechanism here is claimed to make cheating impossible.** What was claimed,
had it been built, is narrower and checkable: a disconnection stops costing the
hand when eligible helpers are present, and costs exactly one aborted hand with
every chip restored when they are not.

### What actually ships, since this is withdrawn

The second half of that sentence, and only it. A disconnection costs one hand.
Every chip goes back. The tournament plays on, and no seat is removed for it —
which is D-010, and is why the cost of the withdrawal is small.

## D-018 — Twenty-three normative terms used and never defined, and what happens to each

Found 2026-08-29 by reading every normative source for the table-formation path
in parallel and checking each against the code, rather than implementing from a
single reading.

### Why this is a decision and not a bug list

`role_code` was normative, undefined, and unnoticed for seven passes, because
the construction that used it **reads complete**. So does every entry below. A
term that looks defined elsewhere is invisible to a reader and fatal to a second
implementation, and the failure it produces — two conforming clients that cannot
agree and cannot say why — has no error message and nothing to attribute.

The rule this establishes: **a normative term is defined in its owning document
before code depends on it.** Where the code has to move first, the guess is
written down as a guess.

### Closed here, with the reasoning in the owning document

| Term | Disposition |
|---|---|
| **U1** `stack_at_hand_start[s]` at `k = 0` | **The ratified roster's `SeatEntry.buyin`** (§3.1). The severe one: it was defined only as `TERMINAL(k-1)`'s final stacks, `TERMINAL(-1)` does not exist, and the value feeds `roster_hash(0)` → `session_id` → every hand's `GENESIS(k)`. Two guesses diverge on every event of every hand, silently. `SeatEntry.buyin` is not chosen by elimination: it is signed under the table key, ratified by a collective stage, and in a tournament forced to a single value by §7.2. |
| **U4** `next_deadline_ms` for formation messages | **`0` for the unchained ones, `crypto_step_timeout_ms` for `TABLE_READY`** (§8.2). The field is normative and a wrong value is an invalid event, and the stage-kind table had no row covering any of them. `0` because they arm nothing: the join RPC has its own transport timeout, the handshake is covered once by `HELLO`, and a `PLAYER_LIST` obliges nobody. `TABLE_READY` is the exception because the beacon follows it — which also gains the row it never had. |
| **U8** `SeatEntry.buyin`'s admissible range | **Within the advert's `[min_buyin, max_buyin]`, and equal to `start_stack` in a tournament** (§3.1, in the same paragraph as U1). It had to be closed with U1: an unconstrained buy-in in the roster is an unconstrained starting stack inside `roster_hash(0)`. |
| **U17** `peer_id` uniqueness in a roster | **Required** (§4.3). Every `SeatEntry` carried it and no rule read it — carried and never checked. It stops one node holding several seats, and therefore the accidental case of one person joining a table twice. **It is not one person per seat**, and that is stated where the rule is: two machines present two PeerIds and are indistinguishable from two people, which is Sybil without an identity layer and is outside `SPEC_CS.md` §18. One key per seat and one node per seat are enforceable and enforced; one person per seat is neither claimed nor achievable. |

### Open, and blocking the named work

| Term | Blocks | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **U5** `password_utf8` — no encoding, length, normalisation or trim rule | password-protected tables | High. Two clients normalising differently produce different proofs and the join fails as *bad password*, which is the one diagnosis that will send a user looking at their keyboard. |
| **U11** *"the parameters it joined under"* — never pinned to a stored object | three of §4.3's comparisons | High. `LobbyStore` overwrites the held advert on every accepted re-broadcast, so *"the advert"* is a moving target unless the joiner retains its own copy. |
| **U13** `stage_type` in `stage_hash` | every chained stage | High. The tests already pass event codes, which is a resolution with no documentary backing. |
| **U16** `P(0)` on a `TABLE_READY` stage that has not completed | the whole setup chain | High. Three sections give three readings, one of which is per-receiver. |
| **U18** *"payload bytes, verbatim"* in `table_params_hash` | the digest itself | High. Decoded content or the CBOR byte string as encoded? The implementation here takes the decoded content, which is a guess and is recorded as one. |
| **U19** *"input deck bytes"* / *"final deck bytes"* | `SHUFFLE_PROOF`, `DECK_COMMIT` | High. No serialisation named, and the open deck never appears on the wire. |
| **U20** the canonical 52-card ordering | anything that names a card | High, and circular: `PROTOCOL.md` defers to `CRYPTOGRAPHY.md` and back. `src/poker/state.rs` fixes `rank*4 + suit` and `tests/deck_constants.rs` pins ziffle's open deck; neither is a document. |
| **U2** `banned`, **U3** capability mismatch | two `JOIN_REJECT` reason codes | Low. Both are advisory and a rejection proves nothing. |
| **U6** *"established connection"* | `JOIN_REQUEST` legality | Medium, and circular: it is defined as the post-`CAPABILITIES` state of the very stream the join RPC exists to avoid opening. |
| **U7** seat allocation when `requested_seat` is absent | the founder's own rule | Medium. Nothing binds `JOIN_ACCEPT n(1)` to a request that asked for a seat. |
| **U9** *"a capability covering `max_players`"* | `TABLE_READY` | Medium. `nlhe/2-6` and `nlhe/7-10` exist; no rule maps a seat count onto them. |

| **U14** *"the first `JOIN_ACCEPT`"* as the abandonment anchor | formation timeout | Medium. Founder's first issued or each joiner's first received — the two give peers different absolute deadlines. |
| **U15** *"the table does not start"* | two failure paths | Medium. No message, state or terminal value, and §4.1 ends the table key's authority at `TABLE_READY`, so there is nothing left to re-form with. |
| **U21** *"occupied seat"* | `HAND_INIT` | Medium. Used normatively three times against a status vocabulary that changed when `Absent` was deleted. |
| **U22** *person*, *identity layer*, *per-identity abort count* | the threat model's own scope | Medium. The absence of an identity layer is the stated reason an attack class is out of scope, and nothing says what one would provide. The abort count is named as the entire remaining sanction with no field behind it. |
| **U23** the formation vocabulary of `STATE_MACHINE.md` | the engine's formation phases | Medium. |

### What this does not claim

That the list is complete. It is what six parallel readings of five documents
found, and the method that found it — read every source independently, then
reconcile — is the method that should be repeated for the hand path and the
dispute path before either is built.

## Open decisions

### How to read the identifiers in this list (`Q5`) — two live `P` series, and which is which

**The problem, stated before the table because it changes what the table means.**
Two independent defect series have been using the bare labels `P1 … P8` at the
same time, in the same files, and three of them collide outright — **`P3`, `P5`
and `P8`**. `PROTOCOL.md` contains two different `P3`s: l. 83 *"P3 is settled
here"* is the witness-independent terminal stage, and l. 5833 *"this is `P3`"* is
the hand-deadline floor. `STATE_MACHINE.md` T50 cites *"(P5, T57)"* meaning the
frozen `Diverged` phase, while this list's `P5` was `NETWORK_STACK.md`'s
prohibition. §2.3 cites *"(P8, §9.4, Q6)"* meaning deferred mid-session seat
entry, while this list's `P8` was a disposition error in `D-014-1`. The failure
mode is not confusion, it is an editor **fixing the wrong item** — which is
exactly how `N-4` came to quote a predicate that had been superseded.

**The convention, and it is one rule.** *An item is prefixed with the gate that
opened it, except the first, which keeps the bare labels it has held longest.*

The original `P` labels are load-bearing inside `STATE_MACHINE.md`'s normative

renaming them would falsify the evidence trail. The fourth gate's series is a
year younger, lives mostly in this list, and its cross-references are countable.

each, in one list, and in three of the five the pass that updated one row left the
other saying the opposite. **A hyphen is not a namespace.** New rows take the
prefixed form and no row may be re-opened under a punctuation variant of a label
that already exists.

**The last column of every `S1-` row opens with one of five status tokens, so the queue can be read exactly rather than guessed at.** `OWNER:` the next move is a decision of yours, not a change to this tree. `OPEN:` a fault that is not fixed. `OWED:` the fix is in and a run or a re-measurement is owed before it is accepted. `FIXED:` built, landed, nothing owed. `CLOSED:` disposed of without a change here — by scope, by analysis, or superseded. They were added on 2026-09-06 because the verdict had always been prose and the vocabulary had drifted: fifteen rows carried no verdict word at all, and a grep for *open* counted `S1-H` — which reads **closed** — because its sources name `hand_one_may_open`. | S1-F | **CORRECTED, and the correction is the finding. Ten seats play; what stopped them was a defect in the founder's invitation, not the seat count.** This row first read *“the client cannot play a ten-seat table”* on a measured cliff between eight seats and nine. The cliff was real and its cause was not scale: the founder invited a seat into the Tox group **only from the `FriendConnection` up-edge**, and `invited` is appended to only when `tox_group_invite_friend` succeeds — so a refused invitation was never retried, the one trigger having passed, and the next up-edge for that friend arrives when the connection drops and returns. A seated player sat outside the group until the network happened to hiccup. **Measured against itself.** Nine seats, one machine, quiet, 300 s, same harness, the only difference being the binary — the pre-fix one built from `69964a9` in a throwaway worktree. **Before:** the founder opened 6 hands and finished 3, **seven of the eight joiners were on a genesis the founder never had**, 43.6 s/hand — the table split in two, and both halves reported `TABLE FORMED session=… seats=9`. **After:** every node opened 11 and finished 10, zero settlement disagreements, 15.8 s/hand. The curve with the fix is **3 seats 7.7 s/hand, 6 10.3, 7 11.2, 8 12.9, 9 15.8, 10 14.1** — a gentle slope, ten inside the noise of nine, **one run per point, and that is weaker than it looks**: a later exercise on the game-on-gossipsub build had formation fail in **2 of 5 runs**, so a point in this table could have been a zero rather than a number. Where a size was repeated the figures agree closely (two Tox three-seat runs at 8.6 and 7.7), so the numbers are stable; the table is an unrepeated observation rather than a measured slope. **Two variables had changed and separating them was the point.** The broken nine- and ten-seat runs were also taken while a nineteen-thread `cargo test` ran on the same machine, which is a measurement fault of mine. Attributing the improvement to the fix without a controlled comparison would have been a guess; the nine clients were separately measured at **0.3 of 24 cores** and 5.8 GB of 31 GB, so contention was never plausible, and the controlled run confirms it. **Two lessons about evidence, and one of them was the instrument's own.** `TABLE FORMED session=… seats=N` is **not** evidence that a seat played — it reports the roster a peer holds, and a peer that heard no hand still holds it; a seat invited at 100 s printed it with the same session id as the seats that were playing, and that line is the pass condition every scripted test here reads back. And **matching genesis hashes are not evidence either**, which the first version of the harness got wrong: `genesis_hand` covers the table id, hand number, session, roster hash, terminal-zero and ratifiers, all held the moment the roster ratifies, so two peers agree on hand N's genesis without exchanging a message. **Opening a hand is local; finishing one is not.** **What is left:** a seat takes 10–40 s to enter the group and once took 125 s, which is friend-connection latency rather than the invitation. | FIXED: `src/tox/table.rs` — **closed**; `pending_invites` is pinned by a test and the seat-count curve is measured to `MAX_SEATS` |

The seat was certified out for not acting, correctly, and is then outside `P(k)`. §4.4 gives `dealt_in ⊆ R(HAND_INIT, k+1) = P(k)`, so it is not dealt into the next hand — and it cannot enter `P(k+1)` without signing a chained event of hand `k+1`, which it cannot do while it is not dealt in. **The corpus names two ways out and neither is implemented.** §4.9's readmission set `A` is written by a seat *signing a chained event*: a `0x0804 PLAYER_SIT_IN` in chain `k`'s boundary window, **or a checkpoint-8 `STATE_HASH` of chain `k` that agrees with this receiver's value**. `PLAYER_SIT_IN`, `PLAYER_SIT_OUT` and `PLAYER_LEAVE` exist only as event-type constants in `messages.rs` — nothing emits or admits them; `BOUNDARY_SEQUENCE_BASE` is referenced by nothing but its own compile-time assertions; and checkpoint-8 `STATE_HASH` is §6.2, whose wire bodies were written today and whose stage does not run. D-013's promise that one silent hand costs one hand cannot be kept by code that has no way to keep it. **It reframes `STATE_HASH`.** It has been queued as divergence detection — §6.1's *“the only way a silent divergence is ever caught”* — and it is equally **the mechanism by which a disconnected player rejoins the game**. That is a stronger reason to finish §6.2 than the one it was queued under, and it makes the boundary-window events (§4.10) the other half of the same job. **BOTH DOORS ARE NOW BUILT, AND THEY OPEN ONTO A WALL THE IMPLEMENTATION PUTS THERE ON PURPOSE.** §6.2's checkpoint runs and agrees across `P(k)` on every hand; §4.9's readmission set is written by an agreeing checkpoint-8 `STATE_HASH`; and since `S1-S` a seat outside `dealt_in` can actually **produce** one, which was the missing link. A readmitted seat's `HAND_INIT` is admitted at stage 0 as an accepted bystander, exactly as §4.9 says. **And it still never becomes required again**, because `next_hand` derives `R(k+1)` by *filtering* `self.open.required` in **both** branches: `R(k+1) ⊆ R(k)`, monotone by construction. A seat outside `R(k)` cannot re-enter `R` however many checkpoints it signs, so §4.9's set widens acceptance for one stage and changes nothing after it. **The corpus's readmission route and the implementation's monotone roster contradict each other**, and until this week that was theoretical because neither end was built. **The monotone rule was adopted for a measured reason** and the code states it: without it a seat certified absent *“came back every other hand and was certified out again, for ever”* — `[0,1,2] → [0,1] → [0,1,2] → [0,1]`. **But that reason may no longer hold, and it is worth checking before the rule is defended.** The oscillation was measured when nothing bounded it. | S1-P | **`Formation::say_again` has never sent anything, in the whole window it exists for. Measured on every node of a run: `said 0 message(s) again, and Duplicate`, thirty-two times.** The mechanism is the client's answer to a real and well-understood failure — GossipSub delivers to whoever is on a topic **at the moment of publishing** and to nobody afterwards, so a roster announced a moment before a peer arrived was never sent to it at all — and it is triggered in exactly the right place, `gossipsub::Event::Subscribed` for the table's topic, on every node. It republishes the **stored bytes** of this client's `PLAYER_LIST` and its own `TABLE_READY`. **And `gossipsub::Behaviour::publish` refuses byte-identical content**: `swarm.rs`'s `message_id_fn` hashes `message.data` and `message.topic` — deliberately, so that one advert relayed by two peers has one id and the duplicate cache actually suppresses it — and `duplicate_cache_time` is **120 seconds**. So the repeat is rejected on the **sender's** side for two minutes after the original, which is precisely the window in which a peer joining or rejoining needs it. After the two minutes it would go out, and for the `PLAYER_LIST` half it is then refused by the receiver instead: `on_player_list` drops a list older than `LIST_MAX_AGE_MS = 90_000`. **Two constants that were each chosen for a good reason meet in a gap no message can cross.** **How it was found, and it needed three numbers this client did not have.** A rejoining client sat at `ratified 1/4, 0 held` for a whole run: its own ratification and none of the other three, nothing refused — a refusal is reported — and nothing waiting, so they never arrived. `Formation::held` exists because `on_table_ready`'s **held** outcome returns `Ok(vec![])` and is indistinguishable from silence; without it, *nobody is talking to me* and *everybody is and I am holding it* read the same. Then the sender's side was made to say what it published, and said `0`. **Why `S1-J` works and this does not, which is the same fact from the other side:** the founder's answer to an already-seated joiner **signs the list again**, so the bytes are new, the id is new, and it arrives — the returning client reports `4 seated` within a second, every run. **And the ratification cannot be repaired the same way.** `emitted_at_unix_ms` is inside `EventBody`, which is what `event_hash` covers, so a re-signed `TABLE_READY` has a different event hash; `session_id` is computed over those hashes, so the receiver would compute a different session identity from everybody else — and `take_ratification`'s *first copy wins* would report an honest seat as `RatifiedTwice`. A ratification must arrive **verbatim** or not at all. **The corpus already has the idiom for that**: §9's join request carries `n(2) advert_event`, *“the complete `SignedEvent` of the `LOBBY_TABLE_AD`, repeated verbatim so the joiner is not relying on a gossip copy and can re-verify the table key's signature itself.”* Carrying the setup transcript the same way — every seat's `TABLE_READY` verbatim inside a fresh message, or in the join answer — is a wire decision and belongs to the owner. **It matters beyond the rejoining case, and that is the owner's own premise:** transport over the internet is unreliable in principle, and during formation every seat's ratification is published once, inside the 120-second window, with the safety net that was written for it inert. A table forms today because the first publish reaches everybody. **Half repaired and measured; the other half is a wire decision.** **The founder's half needed no decision and is fixed**: `say_again` now **signs the roster again** at the moment of saying, exactly as `S1-J` does in the join answer, so the bytes are new, the id is new, and GossipSub carries it. Measured on the next run: `said 1 message(s) again` where every line before it said `said 0 message(s) again, and Duplicate`. A non-founder cannot do this — a `PLAYER_LIST` is signed under the table key — and its own ratification **must not** be re-signed, so a non-founder's repeat is still refused as a duplicate and its log still says so. `a_founder_signs_the_roster_again_rather_than_repeating_it` asserts on the **bytes** rather than the decoded roster, because it is the bytes GossipSub hashes and a test that compared content would pass while the mechanism stayed dead. **And it is not only about rejoining, which is the worse half and was found afterwards.** A seat that joins a table **for the first time** can be permanently excluded by one lost message: measured, `n1` holding `ratified 3/4, 0 held` for a whole run — a complete roster, nothing refused, nothing waiting, **one** `TABLE_READY` simply never delivered — while the other three played fifteen hands and the checkpoint agreed across `P(k) = [0, 2, 3]` without it. A ratification is published once, into a mesh the newest seat may not be grafted into yet, and **nothing ever sends it again**: `say_again` fires on `Subscribed`, which for a peer already subscribed never fires a second time. So a table silently loses seats at formation, and the loss is invisible from every side — the founder counts the seat, the seat holds the roster, and neither has a number that says the session was never computed. **Half repaired again, and the floor is a constant.** Every seat now re-says what it has on the housekeeping tick while `session()` is `None`. Inside `duplicate_cache_time` a seat's own repeat is still refused and only the founder's re-signed roster goes out; after the 120 seconds the repeat is carried. That turns *never* into *about two minutes*, and two minutes at nine seconds a hand is a seat that has missed a dozen of them — so it is a net, not a cure. The case is intermittent and a six-seat run after the fix settled before the first status line, so the net is **not** yet measured catching anything. **What removes the two minutes is a wire decision, and what would let a seat that missed those hands play again is a different thing entirely: state transfer.** Every route here ends at the same wall — the returning client, the excluded joiner, and the seat readmitted by §4.9 all need to know **where the chain is**, and openings are derived locally from the previous hand's settlement, which none of them has. §6.2's checkpoint now runs and agrees, which is the mechanism that could carry it; nothing adopts one yet. In that run the fifth seat was there at 8.4 s, the sixth arrived at **92.4 s**, and hand one opened two tenths of a second later with all six. So the row's own reasoning stands and its conclusion does not: the sweep looked for the right signature and looked at the wrong table size. With the stall applied across the same two machines the retry has nothing to come back to: the founder sent three invitations and logged *“Send handshake packet failed”* at 86, 121, 151 and 181 seconds, and the group stayed at `0 seen/0 confirmed/1 wanted` for the whole run while the recovery spent all three of its attempts. **And the founder-link instrument gave the last piece, which the LAN could not.** Across the two subnets the joiner's link to the founder read **`over a TCP relay`**, where on the LAN it read `direct over UDP`. So a UDP-healthy node marks **zero** relays onion and a UDP-dead one pins `NUM_ONION_TCP_CONNECTIONS` = 3. Three separate mechanisms drive the live count to zero on a healthy node: `kill_nonused_tcp` caps the online set at `RECOMMENDED_FRIEND_TCP_CONNECTIONS` = 3 and wipes the rest; `net_crypto`'s `do_tcp` puts a relay to sleep once its friend link is direct UDP; and a relay that does not confirm inside `TCP_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT` = 10 s is killed and never retried. **And the number this register has been quoting does not mean what it sounds like.** `tox_add_tcp_relay` discards `add_tcp_relay`'s result and answers `true` whenever the hostname resolved, so *“20 of 20 relays accepted”* is a **DNS-success count**, fully consistent with zero live sockets. `toxsink.rs` already says so at the field; the register did not. **PATCHED, AND THE MEASUREMENT BELOW IS WITHDRAWN — SEE `S1-AG`.** The before/after run described here was taken with a far-end binary from the previous day, which had no toxcore log callback in it; the disappearance of the joiner's two errors is explained by that and not by the patch. The reasoning stands, the measurement does not, and it is left in place rather than deleted so the correction has something to point at. **PATCHED, AND MEASURED, AND IT IS NOT A CURE.** `patches/0001-keep-the-tcp-relay-fallback-alive.patch` passes `true` unconditionally — the behaviour the owner reports every other Tox client having, at a cost of three idle relay connections. Two-machine stall test, same shape before and after: **before**, the joiner logged *“Invite confirm packet did not contain any TCP relays”* and *“Got invalid connection info from peer”*; **after**, both are gone — zero `toxcore[` lines on a joiner whose log ran to 3 865, with the diagnostics verified present in the shipped binary. That branch is closed. **The join still does not complete.** The founder now gets past *“no TCP relays to fall back on”* and fails one line later at `send_packet_tcp_connection`: it holds relays for that peer and has no live TCP connection **to them** yet, four attempts over 110 seconds. One obstacle closed, the next visible, the seat still out. **Two patch-free alternatives exist and are recorded rather than taken.** `Tox::tcp_only` already exists and passes `udp_enabled(false)`, which makes upstream's own line call `set_tcp_onion_status(true)` — the same effect with no patch, at the price of putting **all** traffic on relays, which is the opposite of the owner's rule that a relay is a fallback. So the honest reading is the **opposite** of the comfortable one. `add_gc_tcp_relays` having nothing to attach is a general condition of this client rather than an artefact of one wire, and the ninety-second group entry means the twelve-second reaper has **less** margin off the LAN. Shape (i) is a real risk in the wild and this hedge is withdrawn. **And the receive direction shows the C-level skip at the same time.** A healthy seat logged *“Got lossless packet type 0xf2 from unconfirmed peer”* 174 times and *“Failed to create array entry; entry is not empty”* 90 times — packets arriving from a peer that is not confirmed, dropped, exactly as `send_gc_lossless_packet_all_peers` skips them going out. **AND THE PATCH'S COMMENT WAS RIGHT FOR A REASON IT DID NOT STATE: THERE ARE TWO `TCP_Connections` INSTANCES.** A multi-agent read of the vendored tree reported that `set_tcp_onion_status` is never called on the group's instance and concluded the patch *“cannot touch that instance at all”*. The first half is true and worth having — `set_tcp_onion_status` has exactly one call site, `onion_client.c:2193`, on `nc_get_tcp_c(onion_c->c)`, while every chat allocates its own instance at `group_chats.c:7262` — but the conclusion conflates two paths. **The invite confirmation is built from the main instance:** `handle_gc_invite_accepted_packet` fills its relay list from `nc_get_tcp_c(m->net_crypto)` at `group_chats.c:8012`. So the patch acts on the confirmation *directly*, which is exactly what the measurement showed, and the finding was an addition rather than a retraction. The chat's own instance feeds two other things — the DHT announce (`Messenger.c:2458`) and per-peer relay sharing (`group_chats.c:2035`) — and is seeded **once**, by copying main's *connected* relays at the moment the chat is created (`group_chats.c:7249`), behind a refill gate that latches as soon as main's count stops changing (`:7061`). **Which turned that reading into a fix on this side of the boundary.** The founder called `new_group` microseconds after `toxsink` offered the relay list, before one relay had finished a handshake — so its single guaranteed seeding copied **zero** relays and its DHT announce carried none. `HOST_SEED_WAIT` now holds the founder until `tox.connection()` is non-zero, bounded at 20 s so a founder with no network still starts rather than hangs. The events toxcore delivers during that wait are **kept, not dropped**: `iterate` is the only thing that moves `connection()` and also the only thing that delivers events, and a lost friend up-edge is the precise failure the `connected` set was introduced to end. **And the remaining obstacle is traced to a line.** `handle_gc_tcp_oob_packet` (`group_chats.c:6322`) is handed `tcp_connections_number` — the index of the relay the handshake **arrived over**, and therefore live by construction — and never uses it. The peer is bound instead to whatever relay was named inside the packet body (`:5779`), which the founder may hold only as a cold `TCP_CONN_VALID` instance, or not at all. `net_crypto` does not have this gap: it stamps the arrival relay into a pseudo `IP_Port` and calls `add_tcp_number_relay_connection` (`net_crypto.c:1916`), whose own header comment says *“This can only be used during the tcp_oob_callback”*. That is either a log-reading error or a mechanism nobody has named, and this project has already spent a day on a fix aimed at a misread log — so the next step is an **instrumented run**, not a second C patch. **AND THE FIRST MEASURED RUN OF THE SEEDING FIX REFUTED IT IN ONE LINE.** `net::run` advertises a table only once `chat_id_ready` has produced a chat id, and rides the mesh if it does not come — and that timeout was **five seconds** against a seeding wait of **twenty**. The founder logged *“the Tox group did not come up; this table stays on the mesh”* and **no group was created at all**, which is worse than a group with no relays and is the exact failure the fix exists to prevent, produced by the fix. The two numbers are now **one number**: `HOST_SEED_WAIT` is `pub` and the caller derives its timeout from it, so they cannot drift again, and the budget drops to 6 s. **And the predicate was weaker than it read.** `tox_self_get_connection_status` turns non-zero as soon as the DHT answers over UDP, which can be *before* any TCP relay has finished a handshake — and the relays are the entire point of waiting. toxcore exposes no count of connected relays, so `connection()` is the only proxy available; `HOST_SEED_SETTLE` now keeps iterating two seconds past the turn instead of stopping on the first good answer. **Found by running it, not by reading it** — the third time in this session that a change which read as correct was refuted by its first measurement, and the reason the standing rule here is that a fix is a claim until a run has been read. **The harness needed one repair to get that measurement at all**, recorded because it cost a run: `Set-Acl` writes back the whole security descriptor including the audit portion, so Windows demands `SeSecurityPrivilege` and an ordinary shell does not hold it. That is half the rule. `do_gc_tcp` runs every `TCP_RELAYS_CHECK_INTERVAL` = **10 s** and re-seeds the chat whenever main's connected count **differs** from the count the chat last recorded (`group_chats.c:7060-7066`); `chat->connected_tcp_relays` starts at zero and `init_gc_tcp_connection` never sets it, so a group created with nothing is re-seeded within about ten seconds of main's relays coming up. **The seeding is self-correcting, not one-shot**, and it latches only once the two counts agree — which is the state it should latch in. So the wait bought roughly ten seconds of earliness and cost the node loop about six: `tox_sink.start` creates the Tox instance at the moment a table is founded rather than at client startup, so the wait ran *before* the group existed and `chat_id_ready` blocked the whole loop for its duration — precisely while the founder should have been forming its lobby mesh. **Removed.** The reasoning is kept as a comment at the site, because the argument is a natural one to reach again and the ten-second refill is the part that is easy to miss. **If it is ever wanted, the shape is pre-warming** — create the Tox instance when the client starts and only the group when the table is founded — not blocking at the point of use. **Three drafts, and only the third reading of the C settled it:** a twenty-second wait that stopped the group being created at all, a six-second one that blocked the loop for no gain, and then the ten-second refill that made both unnecessary. Every step of that was found by reading the vendored source or by running the thing, and none of it by reasoning from the API. **AND SHAPE (i) IS NOW PRICED, WHICH MATTERS BEFORE ANYBODY WRITES MORE C.** Counted over every run on disk by whether each seat ever printed *"in the table's Tox group"*: **2 seats of 531, 0.38 %**, across 56 runs. **The count was 8 of 538 before one run was thrown out, and throwing it out is the honest move**: `split130526-9` has seven logs, six of them never in the group, and its founder's last line is at **6.4 seconds** — a run that was stopped, not a run that failed. One aborted launch contributed three quarters of this row's whole population. **In the 18 runs dated after 2026-09-05 09:23 — 170 seats — the count is zero, and that is NOT evidence.** At 0.38 % the expected number in 170 seats is **0.6**, so zero is what a healthy sample of that size looks like whether the fault is fixed or not. Eight friendships, membership of the group by its own account, and **not one of the eight others visible in either direction**: every other node's line read `7 seen/7 confirmed/8 wanted` with that seat `silent` for the whole run, rising to `silent 266s`. It opened **zero** hands. So shape (i) is not *a seat that failed to join*; it is **a seat that joined and is invisible**, which is a sharper thing to take to `send_packet_tcp_connection` than the sentence this row had. **And the cost is the whole table.** With that one seat invisible the nine of them opened **zero completed hands in 420 seconds** — the founder opened and aborted five, everybody else opened one and aborted it — where the same rig with no knob at all had just played **62 hands and finished 62** (`S1-BB`). Type 0x00"* — at **42.8, 73.1, 121.7 and 151.9 s**: four failures across 109 seconds, which is the *four attempts over 110 seconds* this row recorded, unchanged by everything since. That line is a **local** peer over the founder's own vEthernet. Checked before it was written, and it is the third time this register has caught an address attributed to the wrong end of a two-machine run. **AND THEN THE OBSTACLE WAS INSTRUMENTED AND IT ANSWERED IN TWENTY-THREE SECONDS.** The failing path was **silent**: `send_packet_tcp_connection`'s only `LOGGER` is an error for a null socket, so the `-1` that matters printed nothing, and the one line that did fire named the request type and nothing else — four failures, four identical lines, no peer. Type 0x00, peer 1057591971, tcp_connection_num 2, **tcp_relays_count 3**, udp ret -1"*. The group believes it holds **three** relays for that peer; the transport's `TCP_Connection_to` for the same peer has **nothing in any of its six slots**. Not handshaking, not killed, not limit-reached — **empty**. So *"it holds relays for that peer and has no live TCP connection to them"* is wrong in its second half: **there is nothing to be live.** The two records are `gconn->tcp_relays_count`, incremented by `gcc_save_tcp_relay`, and the slots in `chat->tcp_conn`, filled by `add_tcp_relay_connection` — and only the first of them happened. That is also why no retry exists: nothing was ever registered to retry. **And the count can never fall back.** `gconn->tcp_relays_count` has **exactly one write in the whole vendored tree** — `++gconn->tcp_relays_count` at `group_connection.c:405` — and no decrement, reset or clear anywhere. **So the disagreement is permanent, and it costs half of every retry:** `try_tcp_fallback` is `handshake_attempts % 2 == 1 && tcp_relays_count > 0`, so on every **odd** attempt the UDP send is skipped entirely and the whole three-second tick is spent on a TCP path that has no slots. Once one relay is recorded for a peer, the founder alternates for ever between a UDP attempt and one that sends nothing. **Not yet established, and the instrument for it is one word short.** `udp ret -1` cannot yet tell *UDP was skipped* from *UDP was attempted and failed*: `ret` is initialised to `-1` and `sendpacket` returns `-1` on failure. Logging `try_tcp_fallback` beside it is the discriminator and is owed. **And the line is too loud as it stands**: `gcc_send_packet` reaches the same function for every group packet, so an unreachable peer produced **1 578 lines in 42 seconds**. **BOTH DEBTS PAID, AND THE DISCRIMINATOR'S FIRST ACT WAS TO REFUTE THE HYPOTHESIS IT WAS BUILT BESIDE.** `udp skipped` is `try_tcp_fallback`, and across `split120422-9` **all four** handshake failures read `udp ret -1, **udp skipped 0**` — UDP was attempted every time and failed every time. The alternation accounts for **none** of them. Without the extra word the register would now carry *half of every retry sends nothing* as a cause, resting on a `-1` that cannot tell a failed attempt from an attempt that never happened. The alternation is still real and still permanent — `tcp_relays_count` has one write in the tree and never falls — but it is not what silenced this peer. **The volume went to the Rust callback rather than to the C**, because the C route needed a mutable `TCP_Connection_to` out of a `const TCP_Connections *` and a cast-away-const is the last thing a reader of a vendored library should find; collapsing consecutive identical messages costs nothing in C, loses nothing — the run is closed by the next different line, which says how many were folded — and quiets every noisy toxcore line rather than the one that happened to be measured. **41 to 646 lines a node against 157 to 1 821.** **AND THE SLOT COMPOSITIONS GIVE THE CHAIN END TO END.** Over the whole run: **1 899** readings of *0 online, 0 registered, **0 other*** — no slot of any kind — and **74** of *0 online, 0 registered, **1, 2 or 3 other***, which is `TCP_CONNECTIONS_STATUS_NONE`, matching the `tcp_relays_count 3` on the group side. So both sub-states occur and the first draft of this reading saw only the first. A slot leaves `NONE` in exactly one place, `tcp_response_callback` — **when a relay server answers a routing request** — and the request is not sent at all if the relay's own `TCP_con` is sleeping or its connection is null. **So a slot stuck at `NONE` means the founder's own connection to that relay is not up**, and a peer with no slot at all means none was ever attached. Both come back to the same place: **this client offers relays to toxcore exactly once**, in `TableSink::start`, one `add_tcp_relay` per bootstrap node and never again — and what it counts is a **DNS success**, not a connection, which its own comment says. A relay that fails inside `TCP_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT` = 10 s is wiped and never retried by anything. **The next step is therefore a behavioural change and it is not made here.** Re-offering relays from Rust was already considered and rejected in this row on the ground that `kill_nonused_tcp` wipes rather than remembers, so a re-add churns sockets — but that objection is about relays killed for being **unused**, and these are needed and not connected, which is a different case the objection does not reach. It is the first behavioural candidate this row has had that is stated in terms of a measurement rather than a reading, and it goes to a refutation pass before it goes into the tree. **IT WENT, AND IT IS DEAD THREE TIMES OVER — AND THE THIRD KILL IS OF MY OWN READING OF THE DATA.** **(1) THE FIX WRITES TO A DIFFERENT OBJECT FROM THE ONE THAT FAILS, AND THIS IS THE MECHANISM THE ROW HAS BEEN LOOKING FOR.** There are **two** `TCP_Connections` instances. `tox_add_tcp_relay` goes to `add_tcp_relay(tox->m->net_crypto, …)` and thence to `add_tcp_relay_global(c->tcp_c, …)` — the **messenger's**. Every group allocates its **own** at `new_tcp_connections(…)`, and the failing send is `send_packet_tcp_connection(**chat->tcp_conn**, …)`. So a periodic re-add from Rust is **inert**, not churny: it cannot reach the pool the failure lives in. **And the way in is closed for exactly the peer that needs it.** A slot on a `con_to` is created only by `add_tcp_connection_to_conn`, reached only from `add_tcp_relay_connection` and `add_tcp_number_relay_connection` — and in the group code every caller needs something **from the peer**: `send_gc_tcp_relays` is gated on `gconn->confirmed`, `handle_gc_tcp_relays` needs a packet from it, and the rest need an inbound handshake or a fresh announce. **A peer's relay slots can only be filled from what the peer sends, and it cannot send until it has slots.** That is shape (i) stated at the transport, and it is a chicken-and-egg rather than a missing retry. **(2) AND *NEEDED* IS NOT A STATE TOXCORE RECORDS.** The rebuttal this row offered — *the objection is about relays killed for being **unused**, and these are needed* — is false on its own terms: `kill_nonused_tcp` defines in-use as `onion \|\| lock_count > 0`, and `lock_count` is incremented only on `STATUS_ONLINE`. A relay a `con_to` wants but has never reached is `lock_count == 0`, which is precisely what toxcore calls unused. **(3) AND THE SLOT DATA SAYS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT I READ IN IT.** Per connection at the founder in `split120422-9`: connections 0, 1, 3, 5 and 7 — local seats that all joined and all reached *are now direct* — read `0 online, 0 registered, **0 other**`; connections 2 and 4 held one slot at one moment each; and **connection 6, the far seat, is the only one that ever held three**, on all four of the handshake failures, every one of which carries `tcp_connection_num 6`. **So having no relay slots is the founder's ordinary state, present in every peer that worked**, and the one peer that failed is the one that had the most. Adding relays cannot be the fix for that. I had this data an hour before the pass and read it as *the founder has no relay for anybody*; the retraction of that reading was right and the reading that replaced it was still wrong. **AND THE INSTRUMENT IS STILL ONE WORD SHORT, FOR THE THIRD TIME ON THE SAME LINE.** `udp skipped 0` does **not** establish that UDP was attempted: `int ret = -1` is assigned only inside `if (!try_tcp_fallback && gcc_direct_conn_is_possible(chat, gconn))`, and the printed field is `try_tcp_fallback` alone. `gcc_direct_conn_is_possible` is *is the gconn's address family set* — so `udp ret -1, udp skipped 0` also means **no datagram was ever handed to the socket, because the peer has no address**. `net_send_packet` returns the length for a routable destination, so a real send would not give -1, and the second reading is the likelier one. `direct possible` is now on the line. **Three discriminators, and each one changed the answer**: without `udp skipped` the register would blame the odd/even alternation; without `direct possible` it would blame a failing UDP send; and the slot counts, read without the per-connection breakdown, blamed the relay pool. **AND THE THIRD DISCRIMINATOR SETTLED IT ON THE NEXT RUN.** `split122952-9`, the same recipe: **all five** handshake failures read `udp ret -1, udp skipped 0, **direct possible 0**`. `ret` is -1 because `gcc_direct_conn_is_possible` is **false** — **the `gconn` has no address** — so no datagram was ever handed to the socket. The reading this row carried an hour ago, *UDP was attempted and failed*, is withdrawn. **So the whole of shape (i) at the transport, in four facts that now all have a line behind them:** the founder holds **no IP:port** for that peer, so the UDP branch is not taken; `tcp_relays_count > 0`, so the *no TCP relays to fall back on* warning does not fire either; the TCP branch is taken and `send_packet_tcp_connection` returns -1 because **no slot is `ONLINE` and none is `REGISTERED`**; and the slots cannot be filled because every filler needs something **from the peer**. **A peer with no address and no relay slot has no way to be reached and no way to acquire either, because both come from the peer.** That is the deadlock, and it is not a missing retry, not a relay pool, and not the odd/even alternation — each of which this row or this session believed in turn, and each of which one more field on one line refuted. **The harness's own note guessed it in 2026-09**: *"the failure turns on the founder having no TCP relays attached to the group connection and on `copy_friend_ip_port_to_gconn` finding no DHT `IP:port`"*. The second half is now measured; the first half is refuted, because the relays are attached and the slots are not. **And that question has an answer, read straight out of the C: the invite rides the friend connection and the handshake does not.** `copy_friend_ip_port_to_gconn` — the one thing `do_handshakes` calls when a `gconn` has no address — reads `friend_conn_get_dht_ip_port(connection)` and **returns false when it is unset**. A friendship that came up over a **TCP relay** has no DHT `IP:port`, which is the ordinary state of two peers on different subnets behind routers — and it is this rig exactly. So the `gconn` keeps no address, `gcc_direct_conn_is_possible` stays false, and the UDP branch is never taken: **`direct possible 0`, measured five times out of five.** **Meanwhile the invite that started all this went through without trouble, eighty-nine times.** `gc_invite_friend` ends at `send_group_invite_packet`, which is `write_cryptpacket_id(m, friendnumber, PACKET_ID_INVITE_GROUPCHAT, …)` — the **friend's own crypto connection**, which is riding the relay quite happily. **So the transport exists, is up, is in use, and the group handshake will not use it.** It wants either a DHT address the relayed friendship never has, or a group relay slot that only the peer can supply. **That is shape (i), complete:** for two peers who are friends **only over a relay**, the group handshake has no path at all, while the invite that created the expectation had one. **And it says what a fix would have to do**, without saying which: either the handshake rides the friend connection the invite already used, or the peer's group relay slots are seeded at invite time from the friend connection's own relays — both are changes to the vendored library, both are behavioural, and neither is made here. What is settled is that this is **not** a retry, a pool, a timing or an address-family problem, which are the four things this row has believed in turn. **AND THEN THE FIFTH THING THIS ROW BELIEVED WAS KILLED TOO, AND IT WAS MINE, AND IT WAS ONE HOUR OLD.** Reading the C for the invite answered a different question on the way: `gconn->tcp_relays_count` has **one write in the whole vendored tree** — the `++` in `gcc_save_tcp_relay` — and **no decrement**, while the slots it claims to describe are zeroed by `rm_tcp_connection_from_conn` every time `do_tcp_conns` kills a relay that never connected. Two records of one fact, diverging permanently in one direction, and **both gates in `send_gc_handshake_packet` read the one the send does not use**: the *no TCP relays to fall back on* warning could never fire once any relay had ever been saved, and the send was skipped whenever the count happened to read zero even though slots existed. Measured at both ends: `tcp_relays_count 3` against `0 online, 0 registered, 3 other`, and **1899** readings of `0 online, 0 registered, 0 other` (`runs/split120422-9`, `split122952-9`, `split115004-9`). **So I proposed swapping the stale count for `tcp_connection_to_online_tcp_relays`, and four independent lenses refuted it on the same ground, which I then read for myself.** That accessor counts **`ONLINE` only**, and `send_packet_tcp_connection` sends through `ONLINE` **and, failing that, out-of-band through `REGISTERED`**. `ONLINE` is reached only on **mutual** routing — `TCP_server.c` sets `status = 2` for both sides at once, when each has routed to the other — which a peer we have **never handshaked with** has no reason to have done. **`REGISTERED`-only is therefore the normal state of a *first* group handshake, and the out-of-band loop is the only path it can take**; `handle_gc_tcp_oob_packet` is registered at `group_chats.c:7696` for exactly that. **My change would have warned and returned false *before* a send that today can succeed** — a narrower gate on the one packet that needs the widest one. `split115004-9` has **53** readings of `0 online, 1 registered` to say those slots are real and not hypothetical. **What landed instead is what all four arrived at independently: keep the count out of the send decision entirely** (`patches/0018-the-send-is-its-own-oracle.patch`). Attempt the TCP send whenever `ret != length \|\| try_tcp_fallback`, and take the warning from `send_packet_tcp_connection`'s own `-1`, which **already means exactly what the warning wanted to say** — neither loop carried it. The attempt set becomes **strictly wider** than before, so **nothing that is attempted today stops being attempted**, and there is no new state, no new accessor and no wire change. **The send is its own oracle.** **And 0018 carries the precondition those same lenses attached, which is the trap this session fell into twice on this row:** 0017's counters live inside `if (!sent_any)`, so a `REGISTERED` slot that **does** carry a packet was invisible, and *"out-of-band never works"* could not be told from *"out-of-band works and is never logged"*. One `LOGGER_DEBUG` on the success side of the OOB loop closes it, and until it has been run under `-Stall` the narrowing question stays unanswered rather than answered no. **One correction to my own chain, from the same pass**: link 2's consequence was wrong. `tcp_relay_on_online` walks every `con_to` holding a relay and sends the routing request once the client confirms — so a newly added relay **does** get one, delayed by the relay handshake rather than absent. The stale count stands; *nothing ever sends a routing request* is withdrawn. **The count for the record: this row has now had five explanations, and the fifth was refuted by the instrument the fourth one built.** **AND THE RUN IS IN, AND THE PRECONDITION IS ANSWERED: OUT-OF-BAND WORKS, AND IT WORKS CONSTANTLY.** `runs/split130525-9`, 8+1 seats, 420 s, the same 30 s stall on the far seat, 0018 in the binary: **135 packets were accepted for out-of-band carriage by a `REGISTERED` relay**, by **every one of the nine seats**, the far one 21 times. A gate demanding `online > 0` before the attempt would have had to be satisfied by slots that were not carrying, and on the likelier reading would have suppressed all 135 sends outright. **The truthful warning fired four times, and only at the founder.** All four are shape (i) exactly as this row diagnosed it: `udp ret -1, udp skipped 0, direct possible 0, target: (IP invalid, family 0):0` — no address, no datagram, and `tcp_relays_count 3`, which is precisely the state in which the **old** warning could never fire. Four different peers, `tcp_connection_num` 5 and 7. **The old string appears zero times in the run, which is what 0018 removing it looks like from the outside.** **And the reading this row must NOT make, for the third time on the same line.** Across the whole corpus the slot counters read `0 online` in **10 916** readings and never once above zero — and that is **not** evidence that `ONLINE` never happens, because those counters print only inside `if (!sent_any)`, and an `ONLINE` slot that carries returns before them. It is the same selection effect that made 0017's *no relay carried* a tautology and that made *out-of-band never works* unfalsifiable until today. What is unconditioned is the 135, and it is enough. **What the run does not settle.** Nine of nine seated, nine of nine entered the group, six of nine finished a hand in 420 s — so shape (i) did **not** reproduce as a permanent invisibility here, and the four failures were transient. This run therefore measures the instrument and not the fault; the deadlock `S1-AQ` records still needs the seat that never becomes visible at all. **AND ONE OF THE TWO FIXES THIS ROW NAMED IS ALREADY IN THE LIBRARY, WHICH RETIRES IT.** The row proposed, without choosing, either that the handshake ride the friend connection the invite already used, or that *“the peer's group relay slots are seeded at invite time from the friend connection's own relays”*. **The second is built, on both sides of the invite, and reading it was the first thing that should have been done.** The joiner, in `handle_gc_invite_confirmed_packet` (`group_chats.c:8444`), copies its **own** connected relays out of the messenger's pool — `tcp_copy_connected_relays(nc_get_tcp_c(m->net_crypto), …)` — hands them to `add_gc_tcp_relays`, which calls `add_tcp_relay_connection(chat->tcp_conn, gconn->tcp_connection_num, …)`, **and packs the same list into the reply**. The inviter, in `handle_gc_invite_accepted_packet` (`group_chats.c:8369-8386`), `unpack_nodes` that list and seeds the peer's slots from it. Both sides then fall back on `copy_friend_ip_port_to_gconn` for an address and refuse the invite outright if **neither** a relay nor an address survived. So *“the slots are never seeded”* was never true, and the corpus said so all along: the founder's four failures carry `tcp_relays_count 3`, which is three relays the **peer advertised** and the founder duly added. **Which moves the obstacle one link further in, and makes it a latency rather than an absence.** A group has its **own** `TCP_Connections`, because NGC routes by the group's key and not the messenger's, so `add_tcp_relay_connection` cannot reuse the messenger's already-connected client: on the new-relay branch (`TCP_connection.c:1481-1491`) it creates a **second client to the same relay**, parks the slot at `NONE`, and returns 0 **without a routing request** — only the already-known branch sends one, and only `if (tcp_con->status == TCP_CONN_CONNECTED)`. The slot reaches `REGISTERED` only after that new client completes its own relay handshake and `tcp_relay_on_online` walks the `con_to`s. **So the first peer to use a relay in a group pays the whole connect latency and every later peer reuses the client** — which is the shape of what was measured: 135 sends carried, four failures scattered through the first 214 s, and every seat in the group by the end. **And it names the next instrument precisely, which this row will not guess at.** `do_tcp_conns` reconnects a relay **only if** it once reached `TCP_CONN_CONNECTED` and otherwise kills it, and `kill_tcp_relay_connection` zeroes the slot on every `con_to`. A group client that never connects is therefore a **one-way door**, and whether that door is what shape (i) walks through is not established by anything in this run — the failures here were transient. **What would settle it is a line at that kill, and it is written now: `patches/0019-count-the-one-way-door.patch`.** The count has to be taken **before** the removals, because `kill_tcp_relay_connection` zeroes every `con_to` and afterwards the answer is always zero — and `rm_tcp_connection_from_conn` already returns the slot index or -1, so it costs one comparison and no extra scan. It sits **inside** the kill rather than at the call sites, so all four callers are covered by one line, and it is silent when nothing was attached, so an ordinary relay rotation does not fill the log and the line means exactly *a peer's transport just got narrower*. `tcp_con->status` tells the callers apart: `TCP_CONN_CONNECTED` is `kill_nonused_tcp`'s announce timeout, anything else is the relay that never connected. **IT RAN, AND EVERY SINGLE KILL WAS THE OTHER DOOR.** `split144000-9`, 8+1, 420 s, the 30 s stall: **12 kills, 30 slots lost, the widest taking 7 connections' slots at once**, on seven of the nine seats — and `status 2` on **12 of 12**, which is `TCP_CONN_CONNECTED`. **So not one of them is the never-connected kill this patch was written to catch.** They are all `kill_nonused_tcp`, and `lock_count` is **0** on all twelve. **And that is the mechanism, because of what `lock_count` counts.** `kill_nonused_tcp` skips a relay only `if (tcp_con->onion \|\| tcp_con->lock_count > 0)` — *“connection is in use so we skip it”* (`TCP_connection.c:1807`) — and `++tcp_con->lock_count` has **one site**, the `status == 2` branch that sets a `con_to`'s slot to `TCP_CONNECTIONS_STATUS_ONLINE` (`:1223-1228`). **So carrying out-of-band traffic for a `REGISTERED` slot does not count as use.** A relay that is doing exactly the job a first group handshake needs — and 0018 measured that job being done **135 times** — has `lock_count 0`, is *“nonused”* by this function's definition, and is killed `TCP_CONNECTION_ANNOUNCE_TIMEOUT` after it connected, which is `TCP_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT`, which is **10 seconds** (`TCP_connection.h:45`, `TCP_client.h:29`). Every `con_to` holding a slot on it loses that slot in the same call. **This row spent a session looking at a door that did not open, and the instrument found the one that does — which is the argument for building instruments rather than reasoning about them.** **AND IT IS THE GROUP'S OWN POOL, WHICH IS THE OBJECTION THAT KILLED THIS ROW'S EARLIER CANDIDATE.** That candidate died because a periodic re-add from Rust reaches `tox->m->net_crypto`'s `TCP_Connections` and the failing send uses `chat->tcp_conn`, so it wrote to a different object from the one that fails. The widest kill measured took **7** connections' slots, which on a nine-seat table is seven of the eight peers at once. **Two honest limits on this reading, both stated before anyone leans on it.** The reaper is **bounded**: `kill_nonused_tcp` returns early unless the number of connected relays exceeds `RECOMMENDED_FRIEND_TCP_CONNECTIONS`, and kills at most the excess — so it is a ceiling on relays, not a scythe, and a peer keeps the recommended count. And **this run is not a controlled comparison**: it also deadlocked — nine seats seated, nine in the group, **0 of 9 finishing a hand in 420 s**, which is `S1-AQ`'s deadlock reproduced under the stall and worse than the same recipe's previous outcome of 6 of 9. Whether the reaping is background noise present in every run or something the stall makes worse is **not answered here**, because every run carrying this instrument so far is a stalled one. A clean run with 0019 in the binary is the baseline that decides it, and it is owed before this reading goes any further. **THE BASELINE WAS TAKEN AT ONCE AND IT DECIDES IT — AGAINST THE READING ABOVE BEING A CAUSE.** `split144804-9`, the identical recipe with **no knob**: nine seated, nine in the group, **24 hands opened and 23 finished on every one of the nine nodes**, and **one** relay kill in the whole 420 seconds — at **419 s**, on one node, taking 7 slots. Against the stalled run's **12** kills from **39 s** onward on **seven** of nine nodes, 30 slots. So the reaping is emphatically **not** background: a healthy table reaps once, at the very end, and a stalled one reaps twelve times throughout. `tools/fold-relay-kills.py` prints exactly this comparison and says so when a run predates the instrument, rather than printing a zero. **And the direction is the thing this row must not get wrong again.** The obvious causal story — *the reaper takes the group's relays, so the handshake has nothing left* — has an equally good converse, and the converse is the likelier one: a group whose seats are not talking sends less, fewer slots therefore reach `ONLINE`, `lock_count` stays 0 on more relays, and `kill_nonused_tcp` reaps more of them. **On that reading the twelve kills are a symptom of the stall and not its cause**, and nothing measured here separates the two. What is **structural**, and independent of which way the arrow points, is the fact the instrument was built to expose: carrying out-of-band traffic for a `REGISTERED` slot never raises `lock_count`, so a relay doing precisely the job a first group handshake needs is *“nonused”* by the only function that decides that word. **That is a defect in a definition whether or not it caused this run.** **What would separate them**, stated so the next session does not have to re-derive it: the reaping is per-relay and the stall is per-seat, so a run in which the kills cluster on the stalled seat's `con_to` before its handshakes fail argues cause, and one in which they follow the table going quiet argues symptom. Patch 0020 is the half of that instrument this row was still missing — 0019's `slots_lost` counts an attachment at **any** status, so *“7 connections lose a slot”* cannot tell seven working out-of-band paths from seven attempts that never registered, and those two readings say opposite things. It now breaks the count down as `(%u online, %u registered, %u neither)`. **IT RAN, AND THE ANSWER IS AS UNAMBIGUOUS AS THIS ROW HAS EVER HAD.** `split150251-9`, the same stall recipe: **13 kills, 37 slots lost, and 37 of the 37 were `REGISTERED` — zero `online`, zero `neither`.** So the reaping is **not** abandoning attempts that had never connected: it takes **exactly** the out-of-band paths, which are the ones 0018 measured carrying group handshakes 135 times, and it takes nothing else. All thirteen are `status 2` with `lock_count 0`, on six of nine nodes, between 90 s and 250 s. **The defect is now measured end to end and the chain has no gaps left in it:** `kill_nonused_tcp` spares a relay only `if (onion \|\| lock_count > 0)`; `++lock_count` has one site and it is a slot reaching `ONLINE`; a `REGISTERED` slot is the only path a first group handshake has; and the slots actually taken are, measurably, **all `REGISTERED`**. **toxcore calls “nonused” a relay whose only slots are the ones doing the work.** **The causal direction is still not settled and this run does not settle it** — it deadlocked as well, 0 of 9 finishing, so the stall's quiet is still available as the explanation for why so many slots sat at `REGISTERED` rather than reaching `ONLINE`. What changed is that the **definition** defect no longer depends on the direction: whichever way the arrow points, a relay carrying out-of-band traffic is invisible to the only function that decides the word *used*. **And the stall's own reproducibility is now three runs deep**: 6 of 9 finishing under 0018, then 0 of 9 twice — against clean runs of the identical recipe at 26 and 23 hands finished on all nine nodes. **The candidate, named and NOT built.** Count a `REGISTERED` slot as use — either by sparing a relay any `con_to` holds a `REGISTERED` slot on, or by raising `lock_count` when a slot reaches `REGISTERED` rather than only `ONLINE`. If that were happening, a handshake failure would follow a kill **on the same node** more often than chance. **It does not.** Across the three runs carrying both instruments, **32 handshake failures and 2 of them fall within 30 s after a kill on that node — against 1.3 expected by chance.** No association at all. **And the counts point the other way outright.** The **clean** run `split144804-9` — 24 hands opened, 23 finished on all nine nodes — has **19** handshake failures and **one** relay kill. The two stalled runs have **6 and 7** failures against **13 and 12** kills. The comparison is built into `tools/fold-relay-kills.py` so the next reader gets it beside the counts rather than having to think of it — a raw count of coincidences persuades, and a count next to what chance predicts does not. **Two limits on my own refutation, so it is not over-read either.** The 30-second window is a choice and a handshake retry interval longer than that would hide an association; and the failures counted need a peer with **no address**, which is the rarer precondition, so the population is small in every run. Seven candidate fixes refuted in one day, the last together with the reading that produced it; what survives is six instruments, four folds, and one booked prediction refuted by its own instrument — the invite confirmation is an accelerant and not a requirement, so *the confirmation went missing* is no longer an account of the seven wild runs; **2026-09-10: the peer-loss shape — 58 s timeout, deletion with exit type 1, a re-handshake that fails after four attempts — was produced on demand for the first time, twice, by a 20 s symmetric outage of one local seat (`S1-CP`), and the mechanism behind it — a phantom sleeper the relay wake path never returns, `S1-CQ` — is fixed by patch 0027; what this row still owns is the join-phase shape, which the fixed run shows untouched: six exit-type-1 deletions at the far seat at 57–73 s, before any window. **The join phase, read with the day's instruments (2026-09-10)**: across the five 8+1 runs the far seat — the relay-only one — reaped unconfirmed peers at 12 s in three (6, 4 and 6 reaps before 100 s; the local nodes 0–1), each *“confirmed 0, handshaked 0, handshake attempts 4–5, last packet 12 s ago”*, each re-added, and every run reached 8/8 confirmed by 61–121 s — the shape costs the join a minute, and in the seven wild runs it cost the seat. In `split132427-9` the far seat's relay slots for the re-added peers were `REGISTERED` again within 0.4–3.5 s and `ONLINE` within seconds (0026), `n4`'s slot for the far seat was `ONLINE` from 50.2 s, both ends' TCP layers carried two out-of-band handshake packets per connection inside the window — and each end's last packet from the other was still twelve seconds before the reap (`n4` reaped the far seat at 59.1 with *handshaked 1, confirmed 0, attempts 4*; the far seat reaped `n4`'s counterpart at 57.5 with *handshaked 0*). Relays up, attempts counted, and nothing reaches the group layer: what the logs could not say is which attempts left — patch 0017 prints only the attempt nothing carried, a routed TCP send prints nothing on success — and why the ones that arrived were dropped, since nine receive-side exits were silent (`handle_gc_tcp_oob_packet` three, `handle_gc_handshake_packet` one, `handle_gc_handshake_response` four, `handle_gc_handshake_request` one). **Instrument, built** (patch 0028, marker 39): one line per attempt with its door, one per silent drop with its reason, one per completed handshake. **Prediction booked before the run** — a plain 8+1 run, read at the far seat's join phase: for every peer it reaps the new lines name where the exchange died, at one end or the other; the falsifier is every attempt carried at both ends and no drop line at either, which would put the loss in the relay between them and the next instrument in `TCP_client.c`. **Two plain runs later (`split135112-9`, `split135613-9`, 240 s each) the prediction has had nothing to read: zero reaps at any of the nine nodes in either run** — the shape that took three of the five knobbed runs of the morning stayed away from both clean ones, so it is not caused by the knobs and not reproducible on demand either. What the instrument read instead is the clean join, for the first time from the far seat's side: its handshake requests to the eight local seats left by UDP at 21.1 s (request type 1), the completed-handshake line printed for five of them at 26.4–27.1 s — **five to six seconds for a cross-network round trip, half the twelve-second reaper's budget** — and every one of the 63 attempts at the nine nodes left by UDP with zero drop lines anywhere. So the shape is a slow round trip losing to a fixed budget, and the instrument that says where the slow half is stays in every 8+1 binary from here on; `tools/read-join-phase.py` reads it. **The third plain run reaped, and the instrument read the cycle end to end (`split140414-9`)** — the prediction held in its falsifier's form: every attempt was carried at both ends and no drop line printed anywhere, so the packets die *between* the ends, and the lines say how. The far seat came late (*waiting to be invited* at 60 s), handshaked with the founder at 76.1 s, and at 76.7 sent *request attempt 1* to the seven other seats **by UDP** — to the LAN addresses the founder's peer list carries, which the far network cannot route; attempt 2 at 79.0 went **by TCP** (the fallback turn: `try_tcp_fallback` is `attempts % 2 == 1`, so UDP and TCP alternate), attempt 3 by UDP again, attempt 4 by TCP at 85.0. Four seats answered the TCP attempt within three seconds (*handshaked with* at 81.3–81.9). Three — `n2`, `n5`, `n7` — never saw any of the four: their own first attempts toward the far seat were *carried by nothing* at 79.9–85.4 s, i.e. they were not yet on a relay the far seat could reach them through, so its out-of-band requests had nowhere to land; the reaper took the three entries at 88.0 s, twelve seconds after 76.0. Then their own TCP requests arrived and the far seat answered — by UDP, to the source address of the request, which routes — and `n7` printed *handshaked with* at 85.2, `n5` at 87.6, `n2` at 90.6: **handshakes completed on entries the far seat had just deleted**, the asymmetric state this row named long ago, now with its cause on the page; the far seat re-added them at 88.8–90.3 and read *7 seen/5 confirmed/8 wanted* at 91.1 s. So the twelve-second budget holds exactly two TCP attempts, the first of which lands only if the target already sits on a shared relay, and half the budget is spent on UDP to addresses that cannot answer. (The reader's *full table at 61 s* for this run was a false read — *group 0 seen/0 confirmed/0 wanted* is a node waiting to be invited, not a full table; the tool now requires *wanted* above zero, and that is trap thirteen for the memory.) **Fix (b), built and booked**: `GC_UNCONFIRMED_PEER_TIMEOUT` 12 → 30 s for this client (patch 0029, marker 40) — a dead entry lingers thirty seconds instead of twelve, which costs nothing, and a live one gets five TCP attempts instead of two. Local behaviour, nothing on the wire. **Prediction, before the run**: a plain 8+1 run in which the far seat reaps **nothing** before 100 s and reads 8/8 confirmed within 20 s of its founder handshake; the falsifier is a reap with *attempts 8–10, last packet 30 s ago* — the same shape, only later — which would mean the target's relay path is the whole story and the timeout was never the lever.
