It read *7 seen/7 confirmed/7 wanted* at 91.8 s and *8/8/8* at 181.8, because the ninth seat, `n5`, entered the group only at 160.7 s — its own line at 150 s says why: *“Tox is offline; of 20 known nodes, 20 bootstrapped and 20 TCP relays were accepted”* — a node whose Tox instance had no DHT for 150 s, so no friend connection and no invite, while the libp2p lobby had seated it at 137 s. That is a bootstrap wait the client already names, not the handshake cycle, and it is the reason the table played five hands in 240 s. So *8/8 within twenty seconds of the founder handshake* had no table to be measured on; the reap census with the patch stands at **0 of 2** — the second run (`split142606-9`) was an ordinary table, nine seats in the group by 70 s, every seat 9 hands opened and 8 finished, the far seat handshaked with the founder at 23.1 s, read *7/7/7* at 61.8 and *8/8/8* at 92.3 with the last local seat arriving at 70.1, and reaped nobody. Against 4 of 6 runs reaping before the patch, 0 of 2 after it; two runs are two runs. The timeout and the instrument stay in the binary; every 8+1 run from here reads itself, and the row closes its transport half when the census has said the same thing a few more times. `split162332-9` (8+1, 420 s, the first run after D-028): 0 reaps again, but the deal came before the group was whole -- n0, n1, n3, n4 and n5 had the full table at 60 s and dealt hand #1 at 58 to 65 s, while n2, n6, n7 and the far seat reached it only at 120 s and opened hand #1 at 90 s -- and hand #1 never ended at eight of nine nodes; what it ran into is `S1-CT`** |

**Addendum, same day.** The last number the Tox question needed is on the status line. `tox_group_peer_join` fires exactly when `gconn->confirmed` flips, which is the flag `send_gc_lossless_packet_all_peers` requires — it skips a peer that is not confirmed and reports success anyway when there are none — so the set that callback reports is **precisely the set a broadcast reaches**. `Tox::peer_count` never checked that flag, which is why `group 3/3` was never proof of delivery and why every reading of that line had to hedge about it. The line now reads `group seen/confirmed/want`: **`seen > confirmed` is the library's skip happening, and the two agreeing rules it out** and leaves the three Rust-side discards — the latch above the publish, the trim that kept the wrong entry, and the early copy with no hold — as the whole explanation. **And on the first run that carried the instrument, they agree.** Ten seats: every node reported `group 9/9 confirmed/9` from the moment its group filled, on every status line. That does not prove the skip can never happen — it is real in the C and the incidence over a wider sample is still unmeasured — but on the runs this project actually makes, **`peer_count` and the confirmed set are the same number**, and the delivery hypothesis that survived yesterday's reading has nothing left to stand on.
| S1-AB | **`PROTOCOL.md` §13 and the code carry two different rendezvous constants under one name, which §14 says cannot happen.** §13 still defines `LOBBY_DERIVATION_STRING = "p2p-poker/mainline-lobby/v1"` and `LOBBY_INFOHASH = fd7c0d69…`, while `run::lobby_namespace` and the rewritten `NETWORK_STACK.md` §3.2 use `"p2p-poker/main-lobby/v1"` → the 34-byte multihash `12207e3429…`. `NETWORK_STACK.md` §14's own rule is *“no value has two names anywhere in the corpus”*; here one name has two values, which is the same defect read from the other end. **This is the one constant on which two independent implementations find each other or do not**, so it is not a tidying job. Found by the `S1-E` survey and not part of it.  **Fixed.** §13 now carries `LOBBY_DERIVATION_STRING = "p2p-poker/main-lobby/v1"` with its 34-byte `LOBBY_NAMESPACE_KEY`, and `RELAY_DERIVATION_STRING = "/libp2p/relay"` with its own — the multihash prefix `0x12 0x20` followed by `sha256(string)`, which is how go-libp2p's routing discovery keys a namespace. The `_INFOHASH` names go with the mechanism that had infohashes. **This was a correction and not a decision**, which is why it did not wait for the owner: the code has shipped these bytes since `56b0b50`, `NETWORK_STACK.md` §3.2 already documented them, and `the_lobby_rendezvous_key_is_the_published_one` already pinned them by asserting the literal bytes rather than recomputing them. §13 was the only place still carrying the old pair, and `corpus_constants` passes either way because it checks the constants the code exports — which is the gap that let this sit: a value the code **stopped** exporting is invisible to a test that walks the code. One thing is worth recording rather than silently kept: the relay derivation string is **not** ours. `/libp2p/relay` is where go-libp2p's own AutoRelay advertises and looks, so a p2p-poker volunteer is findable by any libp2p client and vice versa; a private string would have made this project's relays invisible to the network whose relays it wants to use. | CLOSED: `docs/PROTOCOL.md` §13, and its §7.6 disclosure paragraph, which still quoted Mainline's ~100 hosts per cycle — **closed** |
| S1-AC | **`NETWORK_STACK.md` §4.5's bogon filter has no counterpart in the client, and the attack it names is live: a provider record can make this client dial its own LAN.** §4.5 rule 2 says to drop RFC 1918, RFC 6598, loopback, link-local, multicast, broadcast and reserved ranges from DHT-derived candidates, and gives the reason in terms — *“a record in the public DHT claiming a private address is either pollution or an attempt to make us scan our own LAN”*. **It was never built, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight.** Under Mainline the candidate was a `SocketAddrV4` that application code parsed, so the check had somewhere to live. Under Kademlia the addresses never reach application code at all: they travel inside the DHT messages, go straight into `libp2p-kad`'s routing table, and `DialOpts::peer_id(peer)` asks the swarm to use whatever is there. `run::run`'s provider handler sees a `HashSet<PeerId>` and nothing else. There is no point in the flow where §4.5 could be applied as written. **What it costs is bounded but not zero.** `DIALS_PER_CYCLE = 8` caps the fan-out, `PeerCondition::DisconnectedAndNotDialing` stops a retry storm, and a dial is one connection attempt rather than a scan — so this is a nuisance and a small reflection surface, not an amplifier. But a stranger can spend one provider record to make every client in the lobby knock on a chosen address on its own LAN, and the corpus says that should be refused. **And the obvious fix is the wrong one, which §4.5 itself already knew.** *“This filter is not the same as the publish filter of §5.6 and the two must never be merged”* — mDNS dials RFC 1918 addresses on the LAN deliberately, because two players behind one router is a case this project explicitly cares about. So a blanket refusal of private addresses breaks a supported case. What is needed is a filter that can tell a DHT-derived address from an mDNS-derived one, and `libp2p-kad` does not offer a hook that distinguishes them: the candidate would have to be refused at dial time by provenance the swarm does not record. That is a design question and not a patch. **The design exists, it was adversarially checked from two sides, and neither side broke it.** The provenance signal this row said the swarm does not record **is** recorded: `DialOpts::peer_id(p).build()` sets `extend_addresses_through_behaviour: true` (`libp2p-swarm-0.47.1/src/dial_opts.rs:220`) and every address-carrying builder sets it `false` (`:204`), including `From<Multiaddr>`, which is `unknown_peer_id().address(a).build()` (`:163-167`). `Swarm::dial` then appends what the behaviour returns **only** when that flag is true (`lib.rs:467-470`), and logs a discard otherwise. So a `handle_pending_outbound_connection` that filters what `ipfs_kad` hands back touches the DHT path — `run.rs`'s `DialOpts::peer_id(peer)` — and is **structurally unable** to reach the mDNS path, which dials `swarm.dial(addr)` with the address in the options. That is the property §4.5 demands and the reason its own text gives for not merging this with §5.6's publish filter: two players behind one router must still find each other on `192.168.x`. **Shape:** a newtype `NetworkBehaviour` wrapping each `kad::Behaviour` field, delegating every method and filtering one — about 120 lines, no new dependency, no protocol or wire change. `run::reachable` is already the predicate and is already applied at one narrower site (`run.rs:1885`). Have it count what it drops, because the number nobody has is how many bogons the real Amino DHT actually hands this client, and a filter that counts produces it as a byproduct. **Two cheaper routes were checked and neither works.** `kad::Config::set_kbucket_inserts(BucketInserts::Manual)` governs only whether a peer is added to the routing table **once already connected** (`behaviour.rs:132-149`); it does not gate the addresses a dial uses, so it cannot refuse a bogon. Reading the addresses out of `Behaviour::kbucket(peer)` (`behaviour.rs:714`, whose entries carry `Addresses`) and dialling with `.addresses(filtered)` would set `extend_addresses_through_behaviour: false` and discard the behaviour set entirely — one site, a dozen lines — **but it regresses the ordinary case**: a provider that is not yet in the routing table at the instant `FoundProviders` fires has no readable address, and dialling it with an empty list refuses a peer that is fine. The current code dials by peer id precisely because the addresses may not be readable yet. **Not written.** What is bounded here is a nuisance and one connection attempt per bogon per cycle, capped by `DIALS_PER_CYCLE = 8`; the two findings this pass fixed instead were a mechanism evicting healthy seats and a wire format no second implementation could read. **BUILT.** `Bogonless<B>` wraps each `kad::Behaviour` and filters `handle_pending_outbound_connection`, delegating every other method; `Deref`/`DerefMut` keep every existing `swarm.behaviour_mut().ipfs_kad.…` call site unchanged. **The predicate is deliberately not `run::reachable`.** That one asks *“could the rest of the internet dial this”* and answers **no** for `/dnsaddr/bootstrap.libp2p.io`, which has no IP at all — right where it is used, and wrong here, because using it would have cut names and the bootstrap shape out of the routing table. `not_a_bogon` refuses an address only when it **carries an IP and that IP is somebody's own network**, and keeps anything it cannot judge: a filter that guesses is worse than one that admits what it does not know. RFC 6598 is spelled out because `Ipv4Addr::is_private` does not cover it, and the IPv6 masks are spelled out because `is_unique_local` is unstable. **It counts what it drops**, on the status line and only when the number moves, so *how many private addresses the real Amino DHT hands this client* — the figure nobody had — arrives as a byproduct of the defence rather than needing a second measurement. **AND THE NUMBER IS NOT SMALL.** This row estimated the cost as *“a nuisance and one connection attempt per bogon per cycle”*. Measured, ten seats, seven minutes, with no build competing for the machine: **every node refused between 2 493 and 5 798 private addresses**, median about 3 200 — n0 3 159, n1 2 935, n2 3 682, n3 2 643, n4 3 731, n5 3 195, n6 5 798, n7 2 586, n8 2 493, n9 3 940. The climb is steady rather than bursty: one node was at 771 by its 33rd second and 1 301 by its 93rd. So the public Amino DHT hands this client something like a thousand private addresses a minute, and before 2026-09-02 every one of them entered the dial candidate set. **Stated as an upper bound, because the filter cannot see the one thing that would make it exact.** `handle_pending_outbound_connection` is called on **every** outbound dial, not only DHT-derived ones, and the addresses a behaviour returns are appended only when `extend_addresses_through_behaviour` is true — which the behaviour is not told. So some of those 1 301 would have been discarded by the swarm anyway. What is certain is that `libp2p-kad`'s routing table held that many private addresses to offer, which is the same finding either way: the pollution §4.5 describes is real, continuous, and at a scale nobody had guessed. | FIXED: `src/net/swarm.rs` `Bogonless`, `not_a_bogon`; `src/net/run.rs`; `docs/NETWORK_STACK.md` §4.5 — **closed, and the missing figure measured** |

It is not used for cards.”* So either the seed permutes the seating and `requested_seat` decides nothing that survives the start, or `requested_seat` stands and the seed decides only the button — and the corpus says the second sentence while `PROTOCOL.md` §4.3 and this client implement the first. **Found while verifying `S1-B`**, which is the same beacon and the same missing rule seen from the button's end. **The asymmetry that makes it worth filing separately: a button rotates and a seat does not.** A grindable initial button is worth about one hand of position, because the button reaches every seat. Two colluding players who each name a seat sit adjacent for the **whole tournament**, so one always acts immediately after the other. **But the severity is smaller than that sounds, and the threat model is why — checked rather than assumed.** `THREAT_MODEL.md` already takes as its baseline *“`n-1` of `n` seats are one adversary, colluding perfectly, sharing all”* information. Under that assumption adjacency buys **no information at all** — the colluders already have each other's cards — and what it adds is **acting order**, which is a real edge in poker and a much smaller delta than the phrase *“classic collusion geometry”* would suggest. The threat model does consider the beacon, at row 5 and X6, but X6 is about the beacon's own *reveal-mismatch* failure — a seat that will not reveal — and neither row asks whether `requested_seat` and a seed-derived permutation can both stand. That is not a seat theft — the joiner said *any* — but it is a **grinding surface**: the founder can permute which applicant lands in which seat, which moves `roster_hash(0)`, which moves `session_id`, which moves the button. It is the founder-side twin of `S1-B`'s attack, and it is the sharper reason no cheaper fix than the beacon exists: closing the ratification surface without a beacon would simply hand the grind to the founder, who moves earlier and has `10!` orderings to spend against ten outcomes. Checking it is one comparison on the joiner's side and costs nothing — but it is only worth doing as part of whatever answers the seating question, because if §4.4's permutation wins then the lowest-free rule goes away entirely. **What is not claimed:** that choosing a seat is wrong. At a live cash table a player picks a chair, and §4.3 may be a deliberate import of that. What is claimed is only that §4.4's sentence and §4.3's field are inconsistent, that the inconsistency is invisible today because the beacon does not exist, and that **the moment the beacon is built the two rules collide** — so whoever writes the missing `seed → button` paragraph (`S1-B`) has to answer the seating half in the same breath or the collision lands in code. | OWNER: `docs/PROTOCOL.md` §4.3 `n(4)` against §4.4; `src/table/join.rs` — **open, and it is the owner's; it must be answered together with `S1-B`** |

So a client could vote that a stage had timed out and, in the same breath, refuse a peer asserting the same thing; the abort sat in `self.early` for ever. The cause-1 gate is now `past_deadline \|\| long_past_stage` — **a union, never a replacement** (`past_stage_deadline` is `false` when `owed_type` is `None` and ignores the whole-hand budget, so a replacement would delete the 55-minute backstop and re-create the same deadlock elsewhere), and at **twice** the stage budget rather than once. **The factor of two is not caution, it is the whole safety argument.** An adversarial reading found the 1x version fatally exploitable: a player drawing dead simply stops acting, which manufactures `past_stage_deadline` on every receiver for free, and then broadcasts a bare abort — every seat accepts, the pot is destroyed and the staller is refunded. At 2x the certificate round at 1 % has a full stage-deadline of clear air to seal, force the fold and reset `stage_at_ms`, so the parked abort re-parks. `may_abandon` already used `long_past_stage` for exactly this reason (*“the better mechanism gets to go first”*); the two sides of one rule now agree. Also verified exhaustively: the cryptographic case is never loosened, because only `next_deadline_for`'s action branch can be shorter than `crypto_step_timeout_ms` and that branch is reachable only via `ACTION_GROUP`, which `stage_type` produces only at `Step::Acting`, where `crypto_stage()` is `false` by construction. Second half of the fix: the stall tick now calls `replay_early`, which had exactly one caller — the `Ok` arm of `hand_event!` — so a message parked on a **clock** was reconsidered only by an **event**. **Measured, `split182531-10`, ten seats over two machines: the fork is gone.** All ten nodes in lockstep — five hands opened, four finished, identically on every seat — against `split173908-10`'s 4-versus-10 split. Zero `TooLong`, zero aborts, zero stranded seats. **And the hand that did stall exposed a shape this row had wrong.** Hand #5 hung with all ten seats at *“your turn”* and nothing terminated it. The reason is not a seat that left. **Two distinct subjects each reached 8/9 and neither went further** — digests `@d7280ced` and `@d106bbd3` — and the votes were split across them: `far-n3` cast its votes about seats **0 and 5**, while the majority cast theirs about seats **1 and 7**. Two disjoint opinions about who was holding the hand up, so neither could ever be unanimous. **So unanimity requires the voters to agree not merely that somebody is late, but on who**, and any divergence in `waiting_for()` splits the vote so that no certificate can form. It happened **twice in one run**. **WITHDRAWN: *“and it is not the transport”* was read off a run that was not measuring the transport.** This row said every node reported zero ring-full refusals, zero unhandled packets and zero retransmits. Those zeroes are worthless. `src/tox/mod.rs` registers `tox_options_set_log_callback` **only** under `--features fault-harness`, so a binary built without it writes no toxcore line of any level — not merely no `DEBUG`. The build step added to `tools/table-run-split.ps1` earlier the same day omitted the feature: `split163641-10` carries 155 toxcore lines on `n0` alone, `split173908-10` and `split182531-10` carry **zero on every node**. The events were not absent; the instrument was. The harness now builds with the feature and prints which, and `-Quiet` has to be asked for. **What the same run does support, because it is counted in Rust rather than logged by toxcore, is the opposite conclusion.** The send side is badly behind: `far-n0` reports **404 messages queued**, `n0` **2 481 fragments refused of 6 804 offered** (36 %), `far-n1` 1 854 of 5 638 (33 %), while `n2` and `n4` never report being behind at all. And seats learn it is their turn **178 to 326 seconds** after the deck is sealed, on a link whose measured per-seat latency is 36 to 326 **milliseconds** — seat 0 at 4.5 s and seat 9 at 4.6 s against seat 1 at 178 s and seats 7 and 8 at 326 s. So the divergence that split the vote is downstream of a transport that is minutes behind, which is very nearly the reverse of what this row claimed. **And the refusals cannot yet be attributed**, which is its own defect: `Tox::send` returns the exact `Tox_Err_Group_Send_Custom_Packet` in `Failed::Api` and `flush` discarded it for a bare counter. Code 4 (`DISCONNECTED`) is decided inside `tox_group_send_custom_packet` before any peer is consulted; code 5 (`FAIL_SEND`) comes from the peer loop where `patches/0003` lives. The remedies have nothing in common. The counter now records which. *(An earlier draft of this row named `n0` as the odd one out and cited a `waiting for seat 8` line. Both were wrong: that line came from the `HAND_INIT` stage rather than the betting one, and the per-node counts behind it were of tally lines — votes **received** — rather than votes **cast**. `n0` voted about seat 1 with everybody else.)* **That reframes the remaining decision rather than answering it.** Widening `may_abandon` to originate a bare abort from a betting stage is the obvious way to stop the hang, and it is right in one of the two cases and wrong in the other. Where the table agrees who is late and one voter has merely gone, the certificate would have **forced that seat's fold and the hand would have continued to its rightful winner** — `certify` over an action stage calls `play.round.apply` and `after_action`, it does **not** end the hand — so voiding is a strict loss and it refunds whoever was losing. Where the table cannot agree who is late, the hand is genuinely unrecoverable and voiding is the honest terminus. The two are locally indistinguishable today. And because ordinary packet loss produces the second case routinely, widening `may_abandon` does not merely add a rare terminus: it makes voiding common, which is precisely the outcome a staller who is beaten would choose. **Both failure modes have one source — unanimity is unreachable under ordinary loss — and that is the thing to decide.** Until it is decided, neither `may_abandon` nor a threshold has been touched. **AND IT IS NOW REPRODUCIBLE ON DEMAND, AND THE COST IS EVERY HAND.** `split111706-9`, 8+1, 420 s, one knob — `-Stall 30` on the far seat, which leaves it in the group and invisible (`S1-AA`). They did; the carrier is clean in this failure too. (B) the ping sender does not offer a WAN self address to a peer whose address is on our LAN, and stamps `last_sent_ip_time`, so the interval is an interval. A third hunk — refreshing *direct* on ordinary lossless data — was written, and **withdrawn before it shipped**: a refuter reading the patched tree showed the ordinary lossless path already does that, at `gcc_handle_received_message`; the grep that found the fragment writer had stopped one function short, and the hunk's comment asserted the opposite of the code. **And then the trigger was refuted, and the row has to say so.** The ping-carried address was the working hypothesis for what poisoned n5's view of n0 at 20:34:42, and a refuter excluded it **for that instant, from the code**: n0 received n5's lossless packets directly at 20:34:40.433 and about 20:34:41.5, `gcc_handle_received_message` refreshes `last_received_direct_time` on every direct lossless packet before any other branching, so n0 counted n5 *direct* until at least 20:34:57.5 — and the ping sender carries an address only to a peer it does **not** count direct. The first lost re-send is at 20:34:43.1. For the first fourteen seconds of the fifty-six the mechanism is forbidden by the code it depends on. **So: the two defects are real, `patches/0012` is a guard for a real hazard, and 0012 is not the fix for this run's loss.** What the logs establish is narrower: n5→n0 UDP delivery died between 20:34:41.6 and 20:34:42.8 while n0→n5 stayed alive for the whole window. The cause is **not identified**. Candidates that fit a silent one-way UDP loss between two processes on one Windows host, all open: n0's UDP receive buffer overflowing under eight local instances plus DHT traffic; NAT or firewall connection state; an address change through the handshake path. **The instrument is also weaker than this row first claimed.** Hunk A's refusal line cannot fire within 16 s of a direct packet, so for a fault of this shape it counts nothing. What would decide it next run is two DEBUG lines that do not exist yet: the source `IP:Port` of every UDP packet handled for a peer, compared against `gconn->addr.ip_port`; and every change of a peer's stored address, with old value, new value and caller. That is `patches/0013`, and the refuters extended the list: every change of a stored address with old, new and caller; every packet handled for a peer whose source differs from the address held; each flip of a connection between *direct* and *relayed* and the first blind re-send of a stuck head, with destination and path; transitions of `self_udp_status` and `self_ip_port`; and the two receive-side early returns the enumeration found to be silent. All at DEBUG. Instrumentation, not a fix — and the first run that shows any of them at the moment a pair goes dark is the run that decides this row. **First run with `patches/0013` in, `split235537-9`, 420 s, nine seats:** packets arriving from an address other than the one held **0**, stored-address changes by ping or handshake **4**, direct/relayed flips **64** (one per peer at start is the baseline), first blind re-sends of a stuck head **147**, self-status or self-address changes **11**; stalls **0**, peer timeouts **0**, seats certified **0**, hands **15**. **What those lines said.** The poison happened, live, and to the far seat: at 96 s `far-n0` logged three times *“ping changed a peer's address from 192.168.1.20:3344x to 198.51.100.17:3344x”* — the local LAN's public IP, carried by the pings of three local seats — and `patches/0012`'s refusal line appears **zero** times in nine logs. It could not fire: it refuses only while the peer was heard directly within `GCC_UDP_DIRECT_TIMEOUT` (16 s), and a peer that has been quiet for 16 s is exactly the peer whose address the next ping overwrites. The guard stood aside in the one state that matters. Two more things the instrument showed. Every local node's DHT self-image is the public IP (`… -> 198.51.100.17:port` on all eight), because `ipport_self_copy` prefers the non-LAN echo, so every local ping to a not-direct peer offers the WAN address; hunk B withholds it only when the receiver is held at a LAN address, and on three seats `far-n0` evidently was not. And `far-n0` holds five of the eight local seats at **`172.16.0.1:port` — the far router**, not at 192.168.1.20: the two subnets NAT each other, and all seventy of `far-n0`'s blind re-sends went to those router addresses and were acked in the end. Mixed paths to the same host, then, and the table still played 15 hands with nothing stuck. **`patches/0014`.** The receiver-side mirror of hunk B, with no timer in it: in `handle_gc_ping`, an address that `ip_is_lan` accepts is never replaced by one it does not, and the refusal is logged with both addresses (*“refused a non-LAN address … over a LAN one …”*). A peer we hold on our own LAN cannot be better reached through the public internet, whatever its ping says; the 0012 rule stays behind it for the direct case. The sender now also logs *“offered self address … to a peer held at …”*, so the next run shows both halves of an offer. Wire-neutral like 0012: it changes what a node stores, not what it sends. **First run with `0014` in, `split002630-9`, 420 s, eight seats here and one there, toxcore log on: 23 hands, 23/23 dealt into on every seat, 0 stalls, 0 peer timeouts, 0 certificates, 0 first blind re-sends — the best run of the day by every column.** The refusal fired **24 times, all on `far-n0`, in a 60-second rhythm** (101 s, 161 s, 221 s … 414 s): four local seats — ports 33446, 33448, 33450, 33451 — offered `198.51.100.17:port` and `far-n0` kept `192.168.1.20:port` for each, every minute of the run. The sender's half explains why hunk B never withheld those offers: those four seats logged *“offered self address 198.51.100.17:… to a peer held at (IP invalid…)”* — they hold **no address at all** for `far-n0` and reach it relayed, so `gcc_ip_port_is_set` is false and hunk B, which needs a held LAN address to compare against, cannot apply. The poison was never a direct-timer race; it is the routine `last_sent_ip_time` cadence offering the DHT self-image to a peer the sender cannot reach, and the receiver's rule is the only place it can be stopped. One run against a baseline of one to fifteen stalls in ten of fourteen; it is a sample, not a proof, and the refused-address count is the number to watch across the next ones. **Read the zero on that counter correctly:** it means no ping carrying a different address arrived at a directly-heard peer in those 420 s, so hunk A's refusal was never exercised — the run is consistent with the fix and does not demonstrate it. | S1-BO | **FIXED by `patch 0015`, and it was never as latent as this row said: 44 of the 63 peer timeouts in the day's two bad runs follow a re-handshake on the same node.** An in-place re-handshake resets both message-id counters and the shared key and leaves both rings untouched, so it strands an old-numbered in-flight message, can deliver a stale one under a reused id, and refuses a new one whose slot is still occupied. Found by `S1-BN`'s handshake lens, read line by line and upheld by its refuter, and excluded for `S1-BN` itself on one fact that was true of the nine logs read that day and false of the next two runs: the branch logs *"Handshaked peer ... sent a handshake request; re-handshaking"* unconditionally at DEBUG, and that line appeared in none of those nine. **The lesson is the exclusion, not the mechanism.** This row named its own trigger line and then filed itself as not-firing on the strength of nine logs; two runs later the line was in every one of them. A latent row is only as latent as the last log searched. **The path.** A confirmed peer never re-handshakes on its own — `do_handshakes` skips a handshaked peer — so the trigger is always the *remote* having deleted us and re-added us as a new peer: `do_timed_out_reconn` (private groups, first try at the next 2 s tick, then every 36 s), a sync announce, `load_gc_peers`, or a DHT announce. On the side that receives the request, `handle_gc_handshake_request` recomputes the shared key from the peer's new session key, sets `received_message_id := 1`, and the response sets `send_message_id := 3` (and `send_array_start` with it); the requester's side goes to 2. **Nothing there touches `send_array` or `recv_array`** — the only clearers are `clear_array_entry`, `clear_send_queue_id_range` and `gcc_peer_cleanup` — and `confirmed` stays true, so the application sees neither an exit nor a join. **What that can do.** An in-flight message under the old numbering keeps its slot and its old id in the sender's ring; the resend walk starts from the new counter's slot, so the old entry is not re-sent until the new counter has passed it, and when it is, the receiver — whose expectation was reset small — stores it as far-future or, once the new counter reaches `old_id − 1`, **delivers the stale message as the new stream's next one**. New sends whose `id % 2048` lands on an occupied old slot are refused (`patches/0007`'s *“Failed to create send array entry”*). Packets sealed under the old key that arrive after the swap fail to unwrap, at DEBUG. A `GR_ACK_REQ` for an old id still finds it and re-sends it under the old id. **Measured, 2026-09-05.** The trigger line fires in `split115952-10` on `far-n0` 13 times, `far-n1` 6, `n1` 2, `n2` 1 and `n4` 2 - exactly the five nodes with *Send array stuck* (10, 5, 2, 1 and 2) and no other node; in `split121953-10` on all ten nodes, which is where all ten had timeouts; and in the clean `split094546-10` not once, alongside zero timeouts and zero send-array refusals on every node. **How much of the damage is this row, counted rather than asserted.** Of the 63 timeouts, 44 have a re-handshake before them on the same node and 24 of those are inside one 58-second window of it (median gap 57.6 s in `split115952-10`, 75.6 s in `split121953-10`); the remaining 19 have no re-handshake before them at all, they are the two early bursts between 171 and 192 s, and they stay with `S1-BN`. A gap wider than one window is still this mechanism and not a coincidence - a stale entry only becomes a timeout when the reset counter reaches the slot it sits in - but the honest claim is the correlation, not the arithmetic: the five nodes with the line are the five nodes with the timeout, ten of ten in the second run, and none of ten in the clean one. The chain where it is tight: `far-n1` re-handshake at 406.3 s, refusals from 427.0 s, *Send array stuck* at 459.2 s, the queue draining 2.8 s after that; then 542.4 to 598.2, 664.3 to 719.2, 786.5 to 844.1; `far-n0` 604.2 to 662.7 and 726.0 to 784.3. **The counter that does discriminate is the carrier's own refused-fragment count**, which reached 1406 on `far-n1` and 864 on `far-n0` against 0 on every node of the clean run. *Failed to create send array entry; entry is not empty* does **not** discriminate, and a reader who greps for it will get the wrong answer: the clean run logs 4878 of them and had no timeout at all. **And it does not only lose a message - it stops the seat.** The vendored `gc_send_custom_packet` reports failure unless every reachable peer accepted, and the driver then retains the whole message, so one peer's occupied slot holds a seat's entire outgoing queue until that peer is timed out: 35 to 45 second blocks with the queue climbing to 317 messages, which is what the *transport is behind* lines were saying all along. **One timeout is not this row:** `far-n0`'s four seed timeouts at 181.9 to 183.9 s of `split115952-10` have no re-handshake before them and stay with `S1-BN`'s open one-way loss. **The fix, `patch 0015`.** `gcc_reset_rings` clears every entry of both rings and `last_chunk_id`, and the re-handshake branch calls it and logs the count. Wire-neutral in the strict sense the vendoring rule demands: not one byte changes, and the entries it drops are ones the remote could never have accepted - it reset its own expectation in the same handshake - while the poker layer re-sends the last stages itself. What is owed is a run: the number to beat is 63 *Send array stuck* lines across two runs, and the acceptance is that no such line follows a *re-handshaking* line. **The first run after the patch does not settle it, and the reason is worth more than the run.** `split192124-10` (5+5, 900 s, no fault knobs, the patched binary at both ends and the far copy verified by hash) came back clean: ten of ten seats seated and in the group, 17 to 18 hands each, one genesis per hand, no divergence, no timeout - and **zero *re-handshaking* lines**, so `gcc_reset_rings` never ran once. A clean control, and no evidence about the fix at all. **What the trigger actually needs, now that it has been looked for on purpose: an asymmetric timeout.** The branch fires at node X only when X still holds Y as handshaked while Y has deleted X and re-added it. If both sides time each other out, both come back through `peer_add` with empty rings and nothing is stale. So the precondition is one node ceasing to hear a peer that still hears it - which is `S1-BN`'s one-way loss, the very thing that seeded the cascade in the two bad runs, and which no knob in this tree can produce: `-LinkDown` drops the application's table messages and deliberately leaves the transport alive (`src/net/run.rs`, and its own comment says so), so toxcore's pings keep refreshing `last_received_packet_time` and nobody times anybody out. **The instrument this needs is a one-directional receive drop**: a seat that ignores its peers' packets below the application for longer than `GC_CONFIRMED_PEER_TIMEOUT` while still sending to them. **Built as `patch 0016`**: `P2P_POKER_DEAF_AT/FOR` and the harness's `-DeafAt/-DeafFor/-DeafSeat`, entirely inside `#ifdef P2P_POKER_FAULT_HARNESS`, which `build.rs` defines only under the cargo feature, so a release build has no path to it. Load makes a timeout more likely, not less. **D-027 was exercised too, and healed.** Hand #6 opened at two genesis values - five nodes with seat 7 still in R, four without - and four nodes then banked the late certificate and re-opened: *"hand #6 re-opens at genesis a254eb6c with seats [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9] (was 45bf6449 …)"*. The deaf seat did not stall - it fell seven hands behind and **took itself out**, which is the terminus that exists for it: *"this client is out: the table is at hand 7 and this client reached only 4"* at 408.4 s. Its hand #4 is the only genesis that differs anywhere in the run, eight nodes against that one seat, and the seat then stopped dealing. So the bound released everywhere it was asked to, and `far-n1`'s long sit in the loaded run stays what its own status line said it was: a node with five peers silent at once. `vendor **The recv ring is cleared too, and that is the second half of the fix rather than a cost of it.** That ring is the only input to `gcc_recv_pending`, which is the only input to the mid-delivery bit, which is the only thing that holds a timeout vote off a seat that is merely late (`S1-BK`). It looked at first like a protection being taken away from a peer that had just proved itself alive. It is the opposite, and three lines of the vendored source settle it: the same handler resets `received_message_id` to 1 a few statements later, `gcc_check_recv_array` only ever inspects the single slot at `received_message_id + 1`, and `gcc_recv_pending` counts **every** occupied slot. So after a re-handshake exactly one entry is reachable and all the others are dead for good - while the pending count goes on counting them, holding that peer's bit true for the rest of the run and suppressing this node's vote on it at every stage. That is the permanent silence D-026's bound is written against, bought by accident. Clearing the ring removes a lie, not a safeguard; the bit is re-derived from live traffic on the two-second nudge tick, so a peer with anything genuinely in flight sets it again at once. A remedy considered and rejected: latching the bit for a stage budget after a reset would re-create the same false suppression time-boxed, on all ten nodes in a run like `split121953-10`, and would cost a new connection field, an accessor and an FFI entry to do it. **Three more attacks on this patch, and where each ended.** *The clear sat above four `return -1` paths* - connection overflow, an invalid connection, the TCP-out-of-band gate and a public join into a private chat - where the re-handshake never happens and stock loses nothing: upheld, and the call now sits beside `gcc_set_recv_message_id` where the re-handshake is committed, with only a flag set in the branch that notices it. *New sends could land at the old ids in the emptied ring during the three seconds before the response goes out*: refuted in the source, because every `add_to_send_array` is reached through `send_lossless_group_packet`, which returns at its first line while the connection is un-handshaked - and it is un-handshaked for exactly that window. *Clearing the recv ring throws away messages that had arrived and that nobody will send again*: true, and it is the point rather than the cost. `gcc_check_recv_array` picks its entry **by slot index alone** and `process_recv_array_entry` reads the entry's own id only to acknowledge it, so an old entry sitting at the reset index is handed up as the new stream's next message - which is the second harm this row predicted when it was filed, not a delivery worth keeping. | FIXED: `vendor/c-toxcore/toxcore/group_chats.c` (`handle_gc_handshake_request`), `group_connection.c` (`gcc_reset_rings`), `group_connection.h`, `patches/0015-clear-both-rings-on-a-re-handshake.patch`, `tools/build-tox.ps1`, `patches/0016-a-node-that-goes-deaf-to-its-peers.patch` - fixed and accepted |

But its numbers said something better. The spread of open times across seats is a **median 7.0 s** and a seat emits its first deck event **0.2 s** after opening - so on the face of it every late opener should be buried in early frames, and none of them keeps a single one. The reason is structural: **`HAND_INIT` is a collective stage** (`Phase::Init(stage)`, and the hand does not leave it until `waiting_for()` is empty), so **no seat can emit a stage-1 frame of hand `k+1` until every seat in `R(k+1)` has opened it**. A member of `R` therefore cannot be overtaken; the spread is the collective stage waiting, not the table running ahead. It follows that **`next_early` can only ever fill at a client outside `R(k+1)`** - exactly the bystander this row was opened for, and nothing else. The 69 and 66 readings of *0 early frame(s)* on healthy tables are the correct answer, not a miss, and no run of a healthy table can ever be the acceptance. **What that costs the acceptance, stated as a bound.** The bystander must be outside `R(k+1)` **and** still following, and the only road out of `R` is a certificate, which needs silence: every seat in `R` owes something in every hand, so silencing one always stalls the hand it is in and the drift grows with the silence. Certification took **39 s** of it; the adrift latch tolerates `ADRIFT_MARGIN` = 2 hands, **29 s** at this table's 14.4-second hands. So the instrument this needs is not another fault knob but a **slower table** - a delay on each client's own autoplay action, which makes the two-hand wall minutes rather than seconds and leaves the certification time where it is. **And it did not need building: `--autoplay` has taken a millisecond argument since it was written and this harness had never passed one**, so every run in the corpus is a table playing at zero think time - which is also why hands are 14.4 s and the wall is 29. `-Think <ms>` passes it, to every seat, local and far. At 3 000 ms a hand is about a minute, so a fifty-second mute costs the muted seat less than one hand where at full speed it cost five. A run taken with it measures a slow table and its formation and hand counts are **not comparable with the rest of the corpus**; the harness says so in its header. **And the acceptance run came, at the fourth attempt: `split135059-9`, 8+1, 900 s, `-Think 3000`, a fifty-second mute and a twenty-second certificate delay on one local seat. So an advert ask armed the floor and silenced the founder edge in exactly the fast case the edge exists for. The floor is the founder edge's own now. **A second defect, from the next reader: the edge fired on the connection the join request itself had dialled.** The node refuses a `JoinTable` while one is in flight, so that ask was spent on nothing at the exact moment the driver was closest to a seat - and 21 of 524 joiner logs record the founder's connection dying with a request in flight, after which the founder stays connected and no further connection event is ever raised for it, which is this row's own hole reintroduced one level down. The buffer is structurally eight short, and its admission was a **match guard**: full meant `_ => {}`, so every later arrival was dropped - and the last to arrive at a WAN peer is exactly the frame it turned out to need. `Hand::early` then evicted by **arrival** (`pop_front`), which for a client walking stages upward destroys the contiguous run immediately above its cursor; that queue sat saturated at 64 from 510 s to the end of the run. **Both queues now evict the highest sequence and drop an arrival that is itself the highest**, because a client that is behind needs the low sequences first and the high ones are still covered by their emitters' ordinary re-send. Four tests, and they are worth the trouble: the old decision was a match guard inside the node loop, where no unit test could reach it. **What the panel recommends next, and why it is not built yet.** A **wake** - a seat inside `R` repeating its own small stored frames of the running hand, unasked, three times a hand, gated on `seats \ required` being non-empty, which is a function of the signed opening at every peer and is empty at every healthy table. It scored highest of the four but the panel's own instruction is to **land the eviction repair alone first**: if the bystander then completes the hand, `S1-CD` as measured was a receiver bug and the wake is insurance against a hazard this corpus has not observed. **Three things the judges killed, so nobody re-proposes them:** filtering `said` on the running hand id (it silences the terminal and checkpoint repeats the boundary drain keeps **on purpose**); a `said` retention across hands (built on the false premise in (4)); and **terminal adoption** by a bystander, which is a verified break - `on_late_settlement` does not enforce unanimity, so adoption would put `roster_hash(k+1)` and hence `GENESIS(k+1)` on *which copy arrived first*, which is `D-012`'s forbidden position verbatim. **And the cheap end is ruled out in writing:** a pull already exists at the carrier - the stall tick nudges every seat in `waiting_for`, which becomes `gc_send_message_ack(..., GR_ACK_REQ)` and repairs a hole in the lossless ring. Five types with no published cap fall back to `FRAME_CAP` and the doc says which and why. (0 refused, 0 evicted)"* — up from the 32 that were `NEXT_EARLY_CAP` exactly, with **nothing lost**, which is the budget doing precisely what it was sized for and the panel's count of 46 confirmed to within one frame. (0 refused, 0 evicted)"*, replayed the whole cryptographic prologue in six tenths of a second, and **completed the hand** — then four more. So a readmitted seat holds a hand whose `my_seat` is **outside** the set its own late stage requires; the stage closes on the required peers alone; `late.closed` is set from whichever body arrived first. **And `next_hand` does read those stacks** — its `Phase::Aborted` arm takes `late.closed`'s second element when it is `Some`, so they become hand `k+1`'s `stack_at_hand_start`, enter `roster_hash` and enter `GENESIS(k+1)`. The exposure is confined to a settlement the required peers **disagree** about, which `S1-BD` made audible on purpose and which `S1-CI` shows §6.3 cannot then heal. **And the obvious repair is worse than the defect**: gating the arm on `required.contains(my_seat)` would send a readmitted seat to the abort's stacks while every other seat took the settlement's, forking it away from a table it currently follows. That was the change a refutation pass proposed, and reading it through is what refused it. **So what was repaired first was the comment.** **AND THEN THE QUESTION *CAN THE DEFECT BE FIXED WITHOUT THE FIX BEING WORSE* WAS ASKED, AND THE ANSWER IS YES — ONCE THE DEFECT IS STATED PRECISELY.** The defect is **not** *a readmitted seat adopts a peer's body*. In the agreed case every body is identical and adopting the settlement is right; it is what keeps the seat with the table. The defect is exactly one thing narrower: **when the required peers disagree, the seat adopts whichever body arrived first**, which is choosing a side by arrival order — a per-receiver quantity — into `GENESIS(k+1)`. The obvious fix gated on `required` treated the healthy case too, which is why it was worse. **The right fix treats only the sick one: a borrowed body closes the late stage only if every heard body equals the first.** **Built.** `Late` now carries `own` — whether the body is this client's own settlement, carried across by `give_up` from a `Step::Settling` it was already in, or a peer's, adopted because this client never settled — and `disagreed`, set when a later body differs. The close is `late.own \|\| !late.disagreed`. An **own** body is applied whatever the peers say, exactly as a normally settling peer applies `mine.final_stacks`, so `S1-BP`'s behaviour is untouched and its test still passes. A **borrowed** body under disagreement is not adopted: the client keeps the abort's terminal and stacks and says why — *“its emitters disagree, and this client never settled the hand itself, so it adopts none of them”* — while the required peers, who are the ones disagreeing, are freezing the table at checkpoint 8 anyway, so no hand `k+1` is being dealt for it to have missed. **And `closed`'s own doc already said this**: *“set once every seat of the required set has published **the same body**”* — the sentence was in the field before it was in the code, and the code drifted from it when `S1-BD` turned a refused disagreement into a heard one without the closing condition following. **Pinned by `a_borrowed_late_settlement_closes_only_when_the_peers_agree`**, both halves: two required peers' settlements that differ leave the stage complete and **not** closed, `own false`, `disagreed true`, the abort terminal standing and the note saying so; the same body twice closes it with the settlement's stacks and the settlement winning over the abort exactly as before. **Falsified**: closing on `late.stage.complete()` alone — the old code — reddens *“so the stage is complete and NOT closed”* on the disagreeing half. **And the falsification nearly produced a wrong conclusion, which is recorded because it will recur.** After the break was reverted by copying a backup over the file, the test went red **again** under the correct source, and for a minute the fix looked order-dependent. It was not: `Copy-Item` preserves the backup's **older** mtime, so cargo's freshness check trusted the compilation made from the *broken* file and never rebuilt. The draft kept the second and overwrote the first, and `a_disagreeing_late_settlement_is_heard_and_the_settlement_wins_over_the_abort` — `S1-BP`'s test, which asserts the disagreement is **reported** — went red on it. Both now fold the pending disagreement **in front of** their own sentence, so the prefix a reader greps for survives and nothing on the channel is lost. Worth the sentence because it is the general shape: a new line on a shared slot must add to what is there, not replace it, and the test that proves that is the one written for the fact being displaced. **Field run with the fix in the binary**: `split115754-9`, clean 8+1 — 9 of 9 seats finishing, 23-24 hands each, 9 agreed checkpoints, 0 `S1-CK` refusals, and **0 aborts**, so the late path was never entered and the run says nothing about the fix either way; what it says is that the settled path is unregressed. A run that exercises the late path needs an abort-then-settle race, which the corpus produces at about one in ten hands on a stalled table and not at all on a healthy one this short. The first such run to carry the new line will be the first measurement of how often a late stage closes on a borrowed body — the number this row has been reasoning about without. **The second attempt at that measurement missed too, and the reason is worth one sentence so the third does not.** `split121302-9`, a 14 s stall firing **once** with the new line in the binary: 20 hands finished on all nine seats, the far seat *restarted 1 time* and reached `8 seen/8 confirmed` — `S1-AA`'s recovery reconfirmed — and **zero aborts**. A once-firing stall lands **before the first hand**, so it delays a join and aborts nothing; the aborts in the earlier stalled runs came from tables that deadlocked because the knob re-fired for ever. **So the abort-then-settle race needs a seat that goes quiet *inside* a hand**, which is the mute knob's job and not the stall's: a run with `-MuteOnTurn -MuteAt 60 -MuteFor 90 -MuteSeat 3` — silent on its turn for three times the decision deadline — was the next recipe. **And it cannot reach this path either, for a reason that is a measurement of a different row.** `split122104-9`: 21 aborts, **zero settlements anywhere**, zero certificates. | S1-CM | **The outage knob discards what the transport has already delivered, so it cannot model the one thing a brief outage does on the carrier the hand rides — deliver late — and its own doc claimed it did.** `link_is_down` (`run.rs`, `-LinkDownAt`/`-LinkDownFor`) said it simulates *“a seated player on an unreliable connection [who] loses the line for a few seconds and gets it back … which is what a brief outage does to a client”*. Read against the receive path, it is not. Under `D-019` a hand event is a lossless group packet, and toxcore's ring never loses one inside `GC_CONFIRMED_PEER_TIMEOUT` = 58 s: `gcc_resend_packets` (`group_connection.c:715`) re-sends an unacked entry at 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 s from `time_added`, the receiver asks for the head of any gap with `GR_ACK_REQ` (`group_chats.c:6454`, `:6468`), `handle_gc_message_ack` answers with an immediate re-send, and only a head entry 58 s old times the peer out (`:727`). So a seat whose line is cut for less than that receives every frame it missed, late and in order, as soon as the line returns. The knob's receive side — the Tox path's `if link_is_down() { continue; }` and the two GossipSub sites — steps past a frame the ring has **already delivered and acked**, so the frame is gone for good; its send side is closer to the real thing, because `publish_hand` parks what could not leave in `said` and the re-send arm puts it out once `nothing_leaves()` is false. **What the knob models is a peer whose transport forgets what it received while the line was down — GossipSub's semantics, which has no history — and not the group's.** Verified in `split123139-9`: after its 40-second window the seat received `List(NotNewer { got: 8, held: 8 })` re-broadcasts, 107 of them to the end of the run, and not one frame of the hand it was in; the ring had delivered those into the discard thirty seconds earlier. **Consequences.** Every `-LinkDown` run in the corpus measured a permanent loss and not an outage — `split220636-9` among them, one of `S1-BW`'s two failed reproductions — and the case the owner put in scope when `S1-Q` was closed (*“stačí ošetřit krátkodobé výpadky internetu”*: a seated player whose link drops for seconds and returns) **has still never been measured**; the doc's own sentence that *did the hand recover* *“has never had one [an instrument]”* stayed true after the knob was built for it. **The honest instrument for the downlink already exists and was labelled as idle.** Patch 0016's `-Deaf` drops a group packet before the ring sees it (`group_chats.c:6369`, above `group_packet_unwrap` and `gcc_handle_received_message`), so the senders keep re-sending and the seat receives everything at the window's end; the harness said *“-DeafFor must exceed 58 s or nothing is timed out and the knob does nothing at all”*, which is exactly wrong under 58 s — there it is the brief-outage model, and over 58 s it is patch 0015's re-handshake model. The uplink is the half it does not have: a deaf seat keeps sending, which is an asymmetric outage; a symmetric one needs a wire-level mute that drops an outgoing group packet after the ring took it, and that is not built. **Fixed where it can be**: the doc comment says what the knob models and what it does not, the harness's `link` header carries the same sentence, and the `deaf` comment and header say what the window under 58 s measures. **The prediction for the first brief-outage run is booked before it is taken**, `-DeafSeat 3 -DeafAt 240 -DeafFor 20` on the 8+1 rig: 20 s is under both the 30 s action deadline and the 30 s crypto budget, so no vote about node `n3` completes and no abort is caused; the backlog drains within about two seconds of the window's end; and `n3` finishes as many hands as the other eight, give or take the cut-off. The falsifier is the same run showing a certificate about `n3`, an abort inside the window, or `n3` behind by more than one hand — which would mean the ring did not replay and the deaf drop is no better than the knob. **Taken, and the falsifier fired — for a reason the prediction had not priced.** `split162916-9`: a certificate about `n3` (seat 5 in that run) at 350.0 s, the abort at 359.5, 16 hands against 20. The ring *did* replay — every missed frame arrived, late and in order, the first at 352.3 s — so the deaf drop is the right instrument and the prediction's middle clause was the wrong one: *“within about two seconds”* was twelve seconds from the window's end, because the receiver drains a gap **one message per second**. That is a transport defect this row's reasoning walked past while reading the very functions that carry it, and it is `S1-CO`, with its fix and a second run. What this row leaves fixed stands: the knob's doc, the two headers, and the instrument labelled as what it is. **One more sentence in the harness was wrong and is fixed with the uplink half (2026-09-10)**: it said *“-Deaf … lives in the vendored C (patch 0016) and works in every build”* and kept `-DeafFor` out of the list of knobs that refuse a binary without the fault harness. A copy of a settlement this client reached itself is deliberately silent: the emitters re-send their terminal for a whole hand, and that would fire on every hand at every seat. `tools/fold-late-settlements.py` counts the line as *missed the 800 ms window*, and the same edit found the fold missing the local abort it was written to count (`S1-CL`). **Design, not built, and the refuters are named first**: route a `HandComplete` for the retained hand to `previous.on_late_settlement` when the retained hand is `Aborted`, and when it closes set `pending_repair = p.next_hand()` — the `S1-BS` repair, which already replaces a running hand k+1 with the retained hand's successor when a late certificate re-derives it — with `S1-CL`'s agreement rule untouched, so a borrowed body still closes only when every heard body agrees. A fragmented message is worse, because `handle_gc_packet_fragment` refuses an out-of-order chunk and stores nothing (`:6241`), so a shuffle of several 500-byte chunks (`MAX_GC_PACKET_CHUNK_SIZE`) comes back chunk by chunk at that rate; and the sender's blind schedule (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s from `time_added`, `gcc_resend_packets`) has nothing between 16 and 32. **Two forms of the fix, the first refuted by measurement before the second was built.** The first form of patch 0024 was a silence probe: after two seconds without a processed packet the receiver asks the peer for its head. Prediction booked in the patch header: first missed frame within three seconds of the window's end, no certificate, no abort. `split164858-9` (same recipe, `n3` = seat 8): the probe fired — 292 lines at `n3`, and `n7` answered *“Re-sent requested packet 2455”* every two seconds through the window, each answer dropped as designed — and the seat still got seat 7's shuffle 12.9 s after the window (14:55:17.3 against 14:55:04.4), `n7` answering 2456, 2457, 2458, 2459, 2460 at 04.9, 06.6, 08.9, 10.6, 13.6; certified out at 351.5–356.8, abort at 359.5, 18 hands against 23. The probe moved the first request earlier and could not move the rate, which the refuted prediction says plainly; its header had also named the wrong falsifier (*“if the frame still arrives at +32 s”* — +32 was never the mechanism), and the patch record says so. **The second form is a burst.** Once a second per handshaked peer, `p2p_poker_ask_for_what_is_missing` (`group_chats.c`, above `do_peer_connections`) asks for every id from the head of the gap to the highest id the peer has ever shown this node — a new `p2p_poker_highest_seen`, written at unwrap before the fragment path can refuse and forget — sixteen at a time, skipping ids already buffered; a peer that has shown nothing but has been quiet two seconds is asked for its head alone. Each request is the standard `GR_ACK_REQ` that `handle_gc_message_ack` answers only when it holds the id, so an unpatched peer on the public network sees nine-byte packets it either answers or ignores, and compatibility is kept. Marker 35 in `tools/build-tox.ps1`, broken and restored. **The prediction for the burst run is booked before it is taken**, same recipe: the first missed frame arrives within three seconds of the window's end; the sender's log shows consecutive ids re-sent within one second right after it; no certificate about `n3`, no abort, `n3` finishes as many hands as the others. The falsifier is the drain still taking ten seconds or more — which would mean the bottleneck is not the request side, and the next place to look is the sender's answer path. **Confirmed, every clause, 2026-09-10, `split120908-9`.** The window fell into hand 16's shuffle round: `n3` (seat 8 this time, the last shuffler) had seats 0–4 by 290.9 s and then nothing; its first burst after the window went out at 311.6 s (*“asking peer 1 for messages 2691..2706 (16 sent, highest seen 2879)”*), the senders answered in bursts at one offset — `far-n0` 2306..2317, `n0` 2778..2788, `n1` 2163..2174, consecutive ids in the same second — and `n3` sealed the deck at 313.0 s, under two seconds after the window's end. The peers had waited for seat 8 about 21 s, inside the 30 s clock: no tally, no certificate, no abort anywhere in the run, and every one of the nine seats opened 22 hands and finished 21. The same outage that cost a seat its place in two runs cost it nothing in the third. `tools/read-deaf-run.py` reads a `-Deaf` run this way — the window, the first frame after it, every certificate, and each sender's answers at their offsets, so a drain and a burst look different on the page; its window arithmetic is approximate because the C anchors on the first group packet handled, which preceded the join line by 4 s here. **What this does not settle**: the uplink half of an outage (`S1-CM`, a wire-level mute behind the ring) is still not built, so a symmetric outage has still not been measured; and the burst's cost on a lossy public link is bounded by construction and now has one reading, from the same run: a healthy seat logged 396–529 requests in 420 s (9–11 B/s of payload, peaks of 7–16 in a second) and the deaf seat 1 051, with a peak of **159 requests in the second its window closed** — eight peers asked for sixteen ids each plus the probes, the designed worst case; the quiet probes that go unlogged add at most one nine-byte packet per peer per two seconds on top. | S1-CP | **The uplink half of a brief outage has never been measured, and the code says it will not repair like the downlink half: nothing pushes a seat's unacked backlog when its peers hear it again.** `S1-Q`'s in-scope case is a seated player whose link drops for seconds and returns — both directions. Every `-Deaf` run (`S1-CM`, `S1-CO`) measured the downlink: patch 0016 drops what arrives and the seat keeps sending. For the uplink the ring's arithmetic is the mirror image of `S1-CO`'s and one step worse. So the peers' quiet probes draw the backlog one id per two seconds, unless the seat has something new to say the moment its line returns. Whether it does is the whole question: after the window its downlink repairs in a second, and if the table is waiting on a frame that is *already stuck in its uplink* — its shuffle, its action — it has nothing new to send, and a multi-chunk shuffle drains for eight to twenty seconds against a thirty-second clock that started inside the window. **Instrument, built** (patch 0025, fault harness only): `P2P_POKER_DEAF_UPLINK=1` beside the 0016 variables makes `gcc_send_packet` (`group_connection.c`) drop this node's own lossless and lossy group packets during the same window, *after* the ring took them, and report success as a cut wire does; handshakes pass, as 0016 lets them pass on the way in; the window and its anchor are 0016's, hoisted to file scope so both halves read one clock, and a send before the anchor exists is not muted, so the anchor is not moved by a send. `tools/table-run-split.ps1 -DeafBothWays`; the `deaf` header says which halves; marker 36, broken and restored. **The prediction is booked before the run**, `-DeafSeat 3 -DeafAt 240 -DeafFor 20 -DeafBothWays` on the 8+1 rig, and it splits on the one fact above: if the seat has something new to send right after the window, the peers see a newer id, burst the gap closed within a second, and the run shows no certificate and the seat level with the others; if the table is waiting on a frame stuck in the window, the peers' logs show *“Re-sent requested packet”* answered **by `n3`** one id every two seconds, the clock runs out, and `n3` is certified out — which would name the sender-side half of `S1-CO`'s defect. The second is the outcome to expect when the window lands on the seat's own shuffle, and the fix it would call for is already sketched: when a peer quiet for two seconds or more is heard again, the sender pushes everything that peer has not acked, sixteen at a time — zero cost at idle, because it fires only on a resumption. Not built until the run says it is needed. **Taken twice, 2026-09-10, and the prediction's first branch held for the local mesh both times**: in `split123725-9` the six local peers and the deaf seat repaired both directions within a second of the window's end — the peers sized the seat's gap from its first new packet and burst it closed, `n3` answering seventeen consecutive ids in one second — and in `split125153-9` the seat had the missed shuffles and sealed the deck 3.7 s after its window. **The sender-side push is not needed and is not built.** What the runs found instead is the far seat: in the first it lost `n3` alone (58 s of silence each way, both timed the other out, the re-handshake failed after four attempts), in the second it lost **six of the eight local peers at once** — each logged 2 000–2 600 *no relay carried this packet* in the minute after the window and timed the far seat out at 332–339 s — and both hands died at the deadline. `n3`, the seat that was actually deaf, kept its far path in the second run. | S1-CQ | **A brief outage of one seat kills the far seat's paths to the rest of the table, because the local mesh's relays wake for the outage and go to sleep when it ends, and a relay going to sleep takes every out-of-band slot on it with it.** Measured twice on 2026-09-10 with the symmetric outage (`S1-CP`, 20 s, one local seat): in `split123725-9` `n3`'s connection to the far seat read *“0 online, 0 registered, 4 other, 6 slots”* from the second its window closed, 1 034 sends found no relay in the next minute, and the pair timed each other out; in `split125153-9` **six of eight local peers** lost the far seat at the same moment of `n3`'s window — `n0` 2 507 failed sends, `n6` 2 603, `n1` 2 199, `n2` 2 236, `n4` 2 167, `n7` 2 038, all timing it out at 332–339 s, the far seat timing six of them out at 334–347 — while `n3` and `n5` kept it. **What the code says.** A seat with no direct route lives on `REGISTERED` relay slots: the relay answered the routing request (`tcp_response_callback`, `TCP_connection.c:1283`), the peer is not routed but out-of-band delivery works, and such a slot **locks nothing** — only `ONLINE` slots `++lock_count` (`:1329`). `do_tcp_conns` (`:1877`) puts a relay to sleep when `lock_count > 0` and `lock_count == sleep_count`, i.e. when every connection-to that locks it is itself asleep; `do_gc_tcp` (`group_chats.c:7662`) sleeps a connection-to whenever its peer is direct and wakes it whenever it is not, every tick; and `sleep_tcp_relay_connection` (`:1130`) kills the TCP client and sets **every slot on that relay to `NONE`** (`:1179`) — the far seat's `REGISTERED` ones included, which then carry nothing (patch 0018's *other*). So the chain, as a hypothesis: the outage makes the deaf seat *not direct* for its neighbours at +16 s, their connection-to for it wake, their relays reconnect and register every connection-to on them, the neighbours and the deaf seat come `ONLINE` on those relays and lock them; the window ends, the seat is direct again, the connection-to sleep, the locks turn into sleepers, and ten seconds later the relays go to sleep with the far seat's out-of-band paths on board. Nothing wakes them for the far seat, because its connection-to is always awake and `set_tcp_connection_to_status(true)` on an awake one is a no-op (`:810`). In steady state the same relays carry the far seat because they hold no `ONLINE` route at all — `lock_count` 0 — and the sleep rule never fires; the outage is what puts a lock on them. **This is `S1-AA`'s family** — the reaper that takes `REGISTERED` slots was measured there (37 of 37) — and this is the first recipe that produces the loss on demand, twice in two runs. **Instrument, built** (patch 0026, marker 37, eight `LOGGER_DEBUG` lines, nothing changed in what is done): the relay sleep with the counts that decided it and what it takes (*“relay N goes to sleep (lock_count k == sleep_count k): … K registered, K of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”*), the wake, the connection-to sleep and wake, the routing response and both arms of the status callback. **The prediction is booked before the instrumented run**, same recipe: within a few seconds of the window's end the local peers' logs show *goes to sleep* lines whose *out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to* count is at least one on the relays the far seat was registered on, no *wakes up* for those relays while the far seat lives, and the peers that lose the far seat are exactly the peers with such a line. The falsifier is the far seat dying at a peer with no sleep line at all — then the `NONE` writes come from the reconnect path (`:1075`) or somewhere unread, and this chain is wrong. **The fix, if the chain holds, is one clause**: a relay that carries a `REGISTERED` slot of an awake connection-to is in use and must not sleep — count such slots as locks in the sleep rule, or check for them in `sleep_tcp_relay_connection`. Local behaviour only, no wire change, compatible with the public network by construction. Not built until the instrument has read. **The instrument read (`split130548-9`, 2026-09-10), and the chain was right about the event and wrong about the slot.** At every local peer, in the second its connection-to for the deaf seat went back to sleep — *“connection-to 7 sleeps (peer direct)”* at `n0` 284.7 s, one node per 0.7 s from `n7` at 276.9 — its relays logged *“goes to sleep (lock_count 8 == sleep_count 8): 8 online slot(s), 0 registered, 0 of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”* and set every slot to `NONE`; `n0` then failed 3 602 sends to the far seat (*“0 online, 0 registered, 3 other”*) and timed it out at 342 s, `n1` 2 247, `n2` 2 557, `n3` 1 378, `n4` 2 620, `n5` 2 852, while `n6` and `n7` kept it — `n6` because its far slot sat on relay 10, which did not sleep. So the losing clause of the prediction is **refuted**: the far seat's slot at the five losers was `ONLINE`, not `REGISTERED`, its connection-to was awake (*“connection-to 0 is ONLINE on relay 0; lock_count 1, sleep_count 0”* at 258.0, never a sleep line for it), and the out-of-band count was zero; only `n3`'s relay 2 showed the out-of-band case (*“1 registered, 1 of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”*). **Which leaves the question the instrument was built to answer: how could `lock_count == sleep_count` hold with an awake peer `ONLINE` on the relay?** One function deeper. `sleep_count` is the number of `ONLINE` slots whose connection-to is asleep; going to sleep adds one per `ONLINE` slot (`set_tcp_connection_to_status`, the sleep branch), and **waking never takes them away** — the wake branch only sets `unsleep` on sleeping relays (`:809`–`:850`); the only other decrement is a peer leaving the relay (`tcp_status_callback`, status 1) or the connection-to being wiped (`:781`). Every sleep-wake-sleep cycle of a direct peer's connection-to therefore leaves one phantom sleeper on each relay it is `ONLINE` on, and an outage is exactly one such cycle at every neighbour: not direct at +16 s, direct again at the end. Eight peers `ONLINE`, seven asleep, one phantom — `lock 8 == sleep 8`, and the awake far seat's lock is covered. An upstream defect in `c-toxcore`, and the reason a healthy table never shows it is that a healthy table never cycles. **Fixed, in two parts (patch 0027, marker 38, broken and restored)**: (A) the wake branch decrements `sleep_count` for each `ONLINE` slot of the waking connection-to, the mirror of the sleep branch — with it a relay an awake peer is `ONLINE` on reads `lock > sleep` and stays awake; (B) a `REGISTERED` slot of an awake connection-to counts as a use in the sleep rule and in the reaper (`p2p_poker_relay_carries_awake_oob`, on 0026's counting helper), for `n3`'s case. Local behaviour only, nothing on the wire. **The prediction for the fixed run is booked before it is taken**, same recipe: at the window's end no relay at any local peer sleeps under an awake `ONLINE` slot — no *goes to sleep* line with `lock == sleep` in that minute — no *no relay carried* storm, nobody times the far seat out and it times nobody out, the hand the window fell into completes, every seat finishes level. The falsifier is a sleep line with `lock == sleep` at the window's end again, or the far seat lost by anyone. **Confirmed on every observable that matters, 2026-09-10, `split132427-9`, with one clause of the wording corrected.** Nobody lost the far seat: **zero** *no relay carried* at every local node in the minute after the window and at the far seat after 90 s, zero timeouts after the window anywhere (the far seat's six exit-type-1 deletions and `n4`'s one are all at 57–73 s — `S1-AA`'s join-phase shape, two hundred seconds before the window), zero certificates and zero aborts in the run, hand 11 — the one the window fell into — over at 298.8 s, and **every one of the nine seats opened 20 hands and finished 19**; the uplink burst worked as before (`n3` answered 1574..1589 in one second). Relays *did* still go to sleep at the window's end — nine lines across six nodes, `n4` *“relay 0 goes to sleep (lock_count 7 == sleep_count 7): 7 online slot(s)”* — and with (A) in place that equality means what it was always meant to mean: every connection-to `ONLINE` on the relay is asleep, no awake peer is on it, it may sleep; the far seat's slot was on none of them, which the zero failed sends prove. So *“no sleep line with `lock == sleep`”* was too strong a paraphrase; *“no relay sleeps under an awake `ONLINE` slot”* is the clause, and it held. Three symmetric runs before the fix lost the far seat three times; the one after it lost nothing. (A) is an upstream defect in `c-toxcore` 0.2.23's `set_tcp_connection_to_status` and is worth reporting there; the report is drafted in `docs/upstream/c-toxcore-tcp-connection-sleep-count.md` with the instrumented lines and the one-hunk fix, and **filed on the owner's word on 2026-09-10 as `TokTok/c-toxcore#3081`** (part A only, against `master`, which carries the same wake branch; from the `qavryxdev` fork, branch `fix/tcp-connection-sleep-count`). The vendored patch 0027 stays until a release carries the fix; on the next toxcore bump, check whether part A is upstream before re-applying it. | FIXED: `vendor/c-toxcore/toxcore/TCP_connection.c` (`p2p_poker_count_relay_users`, `sleep_tcp_relay_connection`, `unsleep_tcp_relay_connection`, `set_tcp_connection_to_status`, `tcp_response_callback`, `tcp_status_callback`), `patches/0026-every-relay-slot-transition-says-what-it-took.patch`, `patches/0027-a-waking-connection-to-takes-its-sleepers-back.patch`, `tools/build-tox.ps1` (markers 37, 38), `S1-AA`, `S1-CP`, `S1-Q` — **measured three times, lost three times; the instrument read the chain and refuted its losing clause; the root is a phantom sleeper an upstream wake path never returns; the two-part fix is built, gated and measured — the same outage that cost the far seat every time cost nothing, nine seats level** |
| S1-CR | **A client does not know after a restart that it left a session unfinished, and a client whose session is over must not keep trying to rejoin it.** Asked by the project owner on 2026-09-10 while `S1-BM` was being built. Today nothing about a session survives the process: no record of the table, the seat, the hand reached or the peers, so a restarted client opens the lobby as if nothing had happened, and a client that lost its table mid-hand has no rule for when to stop looking for it. **What to build.** A session record beside the profile -- `table_id`, `session_id`, `my_seat`, the founder's peer id, the last `hand_id` with its `TERMINAL(k)`, and the last contact time -- written at every boundary and deleted when the session ends (the tournament finished, or this seat left). On start, a record that is present means an unfinished session: the client tries to rejoin it before it does anything else, and **the window asks first** -- *an unfinished game at table X, seat N, stack S: rejoin?* -- while a headless client takes a switch. **When to stop.** The record is dropped when the rejoin finds the session finished, and the client gives up when the table's advertisement is gone AND no peer of the session has been reachable for about ten minutes; until then it keeps trying at the lobby's own cadence. The rejoin itself rides `S1-BM`: a seat that comes back outside the roster with chips asks at the next settled boundary and is dealt into the hand after. **Built 2026-09-10, tests first (D-029), and the rejoin needed one thing the register had not seen: a hand.** A restarted client re-entered the group before this (`S1-O` measured it), and then held nothing -- hand 1 from formation is the wrong hand, and there was no other. `Opening::adopt` takes the running hand from a strict majority of the members' own `HAND_INIT` copies at one genesis (the parent is the genesis, the body the stacks and positions, the signers the required set, the roster hash and the blind schedule checked), the decisive test follows an adopted hand as a bystander to the members' own checkpoint, and the node adopts every hand until D-028's return has dealt the seat back in. The record, the window's question, `--resume`, the give-up rule and the founder's refusal are as designed above.
